one_line_idea: Synthetic-data gains in semantic segmentation concentrate on boundary and thin-structure pixels, so pixel-perfect labels rather than scene realism are the active ingredient.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets provide pixel-perfect segmentation masks while human annotations are imprecise near object boundaries, yet reported synthetic-data gains are aggregate mIoU without any spatial decomposition of where the improvement lands.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Most of the transfer gain from adding synthetic segmentation data to real training comes from boundary-band and thin-structure pixels where human labels are noisy, not from region interiors where human labels are already reliable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing mIoU improvements into boundary-band and interior components will show a disproportionate share of the synthetic-data gain in the boundary band, and the gain will shrink substantially when synthetic masks are deliberately degraded to mimic human boundary noise.
why_important: If the gain is boundary-localized, cheap synthetic pipelines that only get geometry and boundaries right could replace expensive photorealistic full-scene rendering, changing where synthetic-data budgets should go.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary-quality metrics exist in segmentation evaluation, but a causal decomposition of synthetic-data gains into label-precision versus content-diversity channels may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched segmentation models on real-only versus real-plus-synthetic data, evaluate with a boundary-band versus interior IoU decomposition on a real test set, then repeat with synthetic masks corrupted to human-level boundary noise and compare the residual gain.
main_risk: Boundary-band pixels are a small fraction of total pixels, so the decomposition needs per-class normalization and confidence intervals to avoid over-reading small absolute differences.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic segmentation data is assumed to help mainly by adding scene and appearance diversity, with label precision treated as an incidental side benefit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If label precision is the dominant channel, then investment in photorealism is misallocated and boundary-accurate crude rendering is the efficient frontier for dense-task synthesis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One real dataset, one synthetic dataset, two training runs, and a boundary-band evaluation script; comparing the spatial profile of the gain is a single-GPU, day-scale experiment.

one_line_idea: Mixing pixel-perfect synthetic labels with convention-noisy human labels creates conflicting supervision that caps segmentation performance, and harmonizing label conventions recovers the loss.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic renderers label exactly the visible geometry, while human annotation guidelines encode conventions such as including occluders, smoothing boundaries, or merging thin gaps; models are routinely trained on both sources jointly without reconciling these conventions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A measurable part of the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction is label-convention conflict rather than appearance gap, and the model internally averages the two conventions, hurting evaluation under either convention.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Explicitly transforming synthetic masks to match the human annotation convention (or conditioning the model on a source flag) will improve real-test performance over naive mixing at identical data and compute, with the effect concentrated near occlusions and boundaries.
why_important: Label-convention harmonization is nearly free compared to improving renderers, so if it accounts for a meaningful share of the gap, it is one of the cheapest available sim-to-real interventions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Domain gap work overwhelmingly targets appearance; treating annotation convention as a first-class domain axis with an explicit harmonization operator appears under-explored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Write a convention-transformation function for synthetic masks informed by the target dataset annotation guidelines, train with and without it at fixed data budget, and compare on real validation data, plus a source-flag conditioning ablation.
main_risk: Convention transformations are dataset-specific and partly subjective, so the result may not generalize across benchmarks without a per-dataset engineering effort.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The sim-to-real gap is assumed to be dominated by appearance and content mismatch, with label conventions rarely mentioned as a cause.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Labels define the target function itself; two label conventions define two different tasks, and no amount of appearance adaptation can fix a target-function mismatch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train one model on naively mixed data and one on source-flag-conditioned data, then evaluate with each convention head; a flip in relative performance is detectable in two short training runs.

one_line_idea: Optical flow transfer from synthetic training data is governed by motion statistics rather than photorealism, so matching real motion distributions with crude rendering beats photorealistic data with mismatched motion.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Optical flow models are trained predominantly on synthetic data because dense real flow ground truth is nearly impossible to collect, yet the generation pipelines emphasize visual realism while motion fields are chosen by ad hoc heuristics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The transfer-relevant factor in synthetic flow data is the distribution of motion magnitudes, discontinuities, and occlusion events, and appearance realism is second-order once basic texture variety exists.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A 2x2 factorial experiment crossing motion statistics (matched versus mismatched to a real target) with rendering fidelity (high versus low) will show a larger main effect for motion statistics than for rendering fidelity on real-video flow evaluation.
why_important: Flow data generation budgets currently go into rendering; redirecting them into motion-field modeling would be cheaper and could improve every downstream video task that consumes flow.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual synthetic flow datasets have discussed motion ranges, but a controlled factorial separation of motion statistics from appearance realism may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build one procedural generator where motion-field distribution and rendering quality are independent knobs, train a fixed flow architecture in the four cells, and evaluate on real benchmark videos.
main_risk: Estimating the real motion distribution requires approximate flow from real video, creating mild circularity that must be handled by using sparse verified correspondences.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The default belief is that more photorealistic synthetic flow data transfers better, motivating ever more elaborate rendered scenes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flow architectures see motion through matching costs that are already fairly appearance-invariant, so the appearance axis may be mostly absorbed by the architecture while nothing absorbs a motion-distribution mismatch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take an existing synthetic flow dataset, resample it to match versus mismatch the target motion-magnitude histogram at equal size, train briefly, and compare real-data endpoint error.

one_line_idea: Metric depth transfer from synthetic data fails primarily because of scene-scale and layout distribution mismatch, not appearance gap, and layout matching closes more of the gap than image translation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Monocular depth models trained on synthetic data typically transfer relative depth reasonably but struggle with metric scale on real data, and the standard diagnosis is appearance domain gap addressed by style transfer or adaptation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Metric failure is dominated by mismatch in the joint distribution of room sizes, object scales, and camera heights between synthetic scene generators and real capture, which no appearance-level intervention can fix.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Resampling or re-generating synthetic scenes to match the target layout statistics (camera height, scene depth range, object size priors) will reduce metric depth error on real data more than an equally expensive appearance-translation intervention.
why_important: Metric depth is the deployment-relevant quantity for robotics and AR; if the community is fixing the wrong axis, substantial effort in appearance adaptation is wasted.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layout statistics are occasionally mentioned in synthetic dataset papers, but a controlled comparison of layout matching versus appearance matching for metric depth may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: With one procedural indoor generator, produce a layout-matched and a layout-mismatched variant at equal appearance quality, train identical depth networks, and compare scale-sensitive metrics on real test data against a style-translated baseline.
main_risk: Layout statistics of real target data must be estimated from limited metadata, and errors in that estimate could mask the effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The sim-to-real conversation for depth centers on making renders look real, with geometric distribution matching treated as an afterthought.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale inference is known to rely on scene priors like typical object sizes; if the priors in training data are wrong, the model learns a systematically biased scale decoder regardless of how real the pixels look.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Stratify an existing synthetic depth dataset by camera height and scene scale, train on matched versus mismatched strata, and evaluate metric error on a small real set within a day.

one_line_idea: For object detection, cut-and-paste composition with mediocre blending matches full 3D rendering pipelines once a low realism threshold is passed, making blending quality an over-optimized axis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Both simple 2D copy-paste augmentation and expensive 3D rendering pipelines are used to synthesize detection training data, but they are rarely compared head-to-head at matched object diversity and count.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Detection transfer depends mainly on object instance diversity and placement plausibility, and blending or rendering realism beyond a crude threshold contributes little, so the two pipelines converge when diversity is equalized.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched instance diversity, category balance, and image count, cut-and-paste synthesis will reach detection transfer performance within noise of a 3D rendering pipeline on real test data, while costing orders of magnitude less to produce.
why_important: If true, most detection use cases do not need graphics pipelines at all, which changes tooling investments for industrial vision teams.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Copy-paste augmentation is established, but a diversity-matched cost-normalized comparison against full rendering for detection may not have been done cleanly.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix an object asset library, produce a rendered dataset and a paste-composited dataset with identical instances and counts, train the same detector on each plus a small real seed set, and compare real-data average precision.
main_risk: Placement plausibility is a confounder: renderers get physical support relations for free, so the paste pipeline needs a placement model to make the comparison fair.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher-fidelity rendering is assumed to dominate naive pasting for detection data, justifying simulation infrastructure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors are trained with aggressive augmentation that destroys exactly the low-level consistency cues that distinguish pasted composites from rendered scenes, so the training process itself may erase the fidelity difference.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use an existing rendered detection dataset, extract its objects, re-composite them onto real backgrounds with basic blending, train the same detector on both versions, and compare transfer in two runs.

one_line_idea: Generative model internals can supply dense correspondence and grouping pseudo-labels for real images, and a student distilled from them can beat students trained on graphics-rendered ground truth.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Diffusion and other generative models trained on real images contain internal features that support correspondence and grouping, while the standard source of dense supervision remains graphics rendering with its domain gap.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pseudo-labels extracted from generative-model internals on real images carry a noisier but domain-gap-free training signal whose net value for dense tasks exceeds clean-but-shifted rendered supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A student trained on generative-feature-derived correspondences over real images will outperform an identically sized student trained on synthetic rendered correspondence data when both are evaluated on real correspondence benchmarks.
why_important: This inverts the pipeline: instead of generating images to fit labels, it generates labels for real images, eliminating the appearance gap entirely for dense supervision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Extracting emergent correspondence from generative features is an active area, but a direct student-versus-student comparison against rendered supervision at matched budgets may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract dense correspondence pseudo-labels from a public generative model over an unlabeled real image corpus, train a student, and compare with a student trained on an existing synthetic correspondence dataset of matched size on a real evaluation set.
main_risk: Pseudo-label noise is structured (systematically wrong on symmetric or textureless regions), and structured noise can teach systematic errors rather than average out.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense ground truth is assumed to require either simulation or exhaustive human effort, with generative internals seen as an analysis curiosity rather than a supervision source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The generative model already paid the cost of learning real-image structure at scale, so its noisy labels encode exactly the domain knowledge that rendered data lacks.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On a small real correspondence evaluation set, compare a probe trained on generative pseudo-labels against one trained on the same number of rendered pairs; a two-day experiment with public checkpoints.

one_line_idea: The value of synthetic data per task is predicted by the cost of acquiring real labels for that task, not by the size of the domain gap, revealing label scarcity rather than realism as the binding constraint.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data shows its clearest wins on tasks like optical flow where real ground truth is nearly uncollectable, and its murkiest results on tasks like classification where real labels are cheap, yet papers explain success and failure through domain-gap arguments.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across tasks, the marginal value of synthetic data is a monotone function of real-label acquisition cost and is largely independent of measured appearance gap, because synthetic data competes against the real-label supply curve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A cross-task audit that regresses published-or-reproduced synthetic-data gains on (a) real-label cost and (b) an appearance-gap measure will find label cost the stronger predictor, and tasks ranked by label cost will match tasks ranked by synthetic-data benefit.
why_important: This reframes when to invest in synthetic pipelines: the decision should be driven by annotation economics, not by whether a renderer can look photoreal for the domain.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The observation is folklore in fragments, but a systematic cross-task quantification treating label economics as the explanatory variable may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select several dense and sparse tasks with public real and synthetic datasets, hold architecture fixed, measure synthetic marginal gain at fixed real-data budgets, and regress the gains against label-cost estimates and feature-space gap measures.
main_risk: Cross-task comparisons are inherently confounded by task difficulty and dataset maturity, so the regression needs many task points to be persuasive.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The domain gap narrative dominates: synthetic data works when the gap is small and fails when it is large.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Where real labels are abundant, synthetic data competes against a strong alternative and loses even with a small gap; where real labels are impossible, even large-gap synthetic data is the only game in town and wins by default.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick two task pairs with opposite label-cost and gap profiles, measure synthetic marginal gain in each at one budget, and check which variable orders the outcome.

one_line_idea: Synthetic scene generators systematically under-produce heavy-occlusion configurations, and matching real occlusion statistics yields more detection and segmentation transfer than improving textures.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Procedural scene generation typically places objects with collision avoidance and visibility constraints for convenience, while real scenes contain dense clutter, stacking, and severe partial visibility.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The occlusion-configuration distribution is a dominant, under-measured axis of the sim-to-real content gap for instance-level tasks, and models trained on occlusion-matched synthetic data transfer better at equal rendering quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Regenerating a synthetic dataset with the object-visibility-fraction histogram matched to a real target dataset will improve real-data instance segmentation and detection more than a texture-and-lighting realism upgrade of equal generation cost.
why_important: Occlusion handling is where dense models fail in deployment; if generators are silently avoiding occlusion, the sim-to-real literature is training on an artificially easy content distribution.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Occlusion-aware augmentation exists, but treating the full visibility-fraction distribution as a first-class generation target with measured matching may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a procedural generator to control per-instance visibility fractions, produce matched and default variants, train identical models, and evaluate on real data stratified by occlusion level.
main_risk: Ground-truth visibility fractions for the real target must be estimated from amodal annotations or approximations, introducing estimation error into the matching target.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Content gap discussions center on asset variety and appearance; occlusion statistics are rarely reported for either synthetic or real datasets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Occlusion is the hardest thing to learn from data that lacks it, and no appearance-level realism can compensate for never having seen an object at low visibility.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Filter an existing synthetic dataset into low-occlusion and occlusion-rich subsets of equal size, train on each, and compare real-data performance on occluded instances specifically.

one_line_idea: For human pose estimation, sampling synthetic poses approximately uniformly over kinematically valid space transfers better than sampling from realistic motion-capture distributions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic human datasets typically drive rendered bodies with motion-capture data, reproducing the pose frequency distribution of capture sessions, while real-world evaluation increasingly stresses rare poses where models fail.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because pose estimation errors concentrate in the tail of the pose distribution, de-biasing the synthetic pose sampler toward uniform coverage of valid pose space buys more real-world robustness than matching realistic pose frequencies.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At equal dataset size, a uniform-in-pose-space synthetic set will lose slightly on average-case real benchmarks but win substantially on rare-pose subsets, and a mixed sampler will dominate both on combined metrics.
why_important: Deployment failures in pose estimation are tail failures (falls, athletics, unusual occupations), which are precisely what mocap-realistic synthesis under-covers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pose-diversity augmentation exists, but framing the sampling distribution as an explicit uniform-versus-realistic experimental axis with tail-stratified evaluation may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render two synthetic human datasets differing only in pose sampling distribution, train identical pose networks, and evaluate on real data stratified by pose rarity estimated from a large pose corpus.
main_risk: Uniform sampling over joint-angle space produces many contorted poses whose renders have self-intersection artifacts, contaminating the comparison unless validity filtering is careful.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Realistic pose distributions are assumed better because they match the test distribution on average.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Average-case pose accuracy is saturated by realistic data anyway, so all remaining headroom lives in the tail where uniform sampling allocates its mass.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reweight an existing synthetic human dataset toward its own pose-space tail versus its head at equal sample count, train briefly, and compare on a rare-pose real subset.

one_line_idea: Synthetic stuff classes transfer nearly for free while thing classes carry most of the sim-to-real gap, motivating hybrid pipelines that render backgrounds and paste real object instances.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Panoptic and semantic segmentation aggregate performance over stuff (amorphous regions) and things (countable objects), and sim-to-real papers report combined scores without systematically separating the two regimes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The appearance and shape statistics of stuff regions are easy to render acceptably, so the transfer gap concentrates in thing classes, where instance-level texture, wear, and intra-class variety are hard to synthesize.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A stuff-versus-things decomposition of sim-to-real transfer will show a substantially smaller relative gap for stuff, and a hybrid dataset with rendered stuff plus real-image thing instances will outperform fully synthetic data at equal size.
why_important: If the gap is thing-concentrated, teams can stop trying to render convincing objects and instead harvest real instances, which are abundant, and use rendering only for consistent scene context and geometry labels.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Copy-paste and rendering are both known, but the stuff-things asymmetry as a measured principle guiding hybrid pipeline design may be unstated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on fully synthetic, fully real, and hybrid (rendered stuff plus pasted real things) datasets at matched sizes, and report stuff and thing scores separately on real validation data.
main_risk: Class-frequency imbalance between stuff and things can mimic the asymmetry, so the analysis must control for pixel share and class count.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The sim-to-real gap is discussed as a whole-image property, and pipelines aim to make entire scenes photoreal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Stuff textures are statistically stationary and easy for renderers, while things carry identity-specific detail that generative and graphics pipelines both blur; the gap should therefore be structurally asymmetric.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-score an existing sim-to-real segmentation experiment with stuff and thing classes separated; if the asymmetry is absent there, the hypothesis dies without any new training.

one_line_idea: A measurable share of the sim-to-real segmentation gap is ontology mismatch between asset-derived synthetic classes and visually defined real classes, fixable by remapping rather than rendering.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets inherit class definitions from 3D asset libraries and game ontologies, while real benchmarks define classes through annotation guidelines; mapping between the two is done once by hand and rarely audited.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Class-mapping errors and definitional mismatches (what counts as road versus parking, building versus wall) contribute a non-trivial, quantifiable fraction of measured sim-to-real error that is misattributed to appearance gap.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An audit that re-annotates a sample of synthetic frames under the real benchmark's guidelines will reveal systematic label disagreements, and correcting the mapping will recover a visible fraction of the sim-to-real mIoU gap with no change to images.
why_important: Ontology fixes are nearly free and permanent, whereas appearance adaptation is expensive and per-domain; the field should know how much gap is claimable by bookkeeping alone.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dataset papers acknowledge mapping choices in passing, but a quantified error attribution of the gap to ontology mismatch may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample synthetic frames, re-annotate them under the target benchmark guidelines, measure the disagreement rate with the shipped labels, retrain with corrected labels, and compare transfer.
main_risk: Re-annotation is subjective and needs multiple annotators to distinguish ontology mismatch from ordinary annotation noise.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Shipped class mappings are treated as correct, and residual transfer error is attributed to pixels rather than to definitions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any pipeline stage nobody audits accumulates error; class mapping is such a stage, and dense metrics are sensitive to even small systematic label shifts in frequent classes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually inspect a few hundred synthetic-real class-confusion pairs from an existing transfer experiment and count how many confusions align with plausible definitional mismatches rather than visual errors.

one_line_idea: Synthetic video with perfectly coherent frames teaches temporal over-smoothness, so video models trained on it degrade on real footage with cuts, jitter, and exposure changes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rendered video provides flawless temporal continuity and exact inter-frame correspondence, while real video contains compression artifacts, rolling shutter, auto-exposure shifts, and editing cuts.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on temporally pristine synthetic video learn to rely on continuity assumptions that are violated by real footage, creating a specific failure mode (over-propagation across cuts and jumps) that appearance-level domain adaptation does not fix.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Video segmentation or tracking models trained on pristine synthetic video will show disproportionate errors immediately after cuts and camera jerks in real video, and injecting synthetic temporal corruptions (fake cuts, exposure jumps, jitter) during training will fix these errors without hurting smooth-video performance.
why_important: Video models are increasingly trained on rendered or generated footage, and a systematic continuity bias would silently degrade all real-world deployments on edited or handheld content.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal augmentation exists piecemeal, but identifying pristine-continuity training as a distinct bias with a targeted corruption remedy may be unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a video model on synthetic footage with and without temporal-corruption augmentation, evaluate on real video with annotated cut and jitter locations, and compare error profiles around discontinuities.
main_risk: Real-video error concentration near cuts could reflect annotation difficulty at those frames rather than model bias, requiring careful ground-truth handling.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic video is treated as strictly cleaner training data, with temporal perfection viewed as an advantage rather than a distribution shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perfect continuity is a strong spurious cue: if it always holds in training, the model will bake it into its temporal prior, exactly as models bake in any invariant of the training set.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take a public model trained on synthetic video, measure its per-frame error as a function of distance from real-video cuts, and compare against a real-trained model; requires only evaluation.

one_line_idea: For depth-sensor tasks, faithful sensor-noise simulation matters more than scene realism, and a cheap noise-model calibration step beats expensive content upgrades.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic training data for depth completion and depth-sensor perception is typically rendered with idealized clean depth, while real sensors exhibit structured noise: edge dropout, multipath artifacts, quantization, and material-dependent holes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant sim-to-real factor for sensor-consuming models is the mismatch between simulated and actual sensor noise processes, and calibrating a noise model from a small amount of real sensor data closes more gap than improving scene diversity or rendering quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At fixed content, adding a calibrated sensor-noise model to synthetic depth will improve real-data performance more than doubling scene diversity without a noise model, for depth completion and downstream grasping-style perception metrics.
why_important: Sensor noise calibration needs only minutes of real capture and no annotation, making it one of the highest-leverage steps if the hypothesis holds.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sensor simulation is a known topic in robotics, but a controlled leverage comparison between noise fidelity and content fidelity at matched cost may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture unlabeled frames from the target sensor, fit a structured noise model, apply it to existing synthetic depth data, and compare student models trained with noise-augmented versus content-doubled data on real annotated tests.
main_risk: Noise models fitted on one sensor unit or scene type may not generalize across devices and materials, understating the achievable gain.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The default effort allocation in synthetic pipelines favors scene assets and rendering, with sensor modeling treated as an optional detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The model's input distribution is the sensor output, not the scene; any mismatch at the input interface hits every example, whereas content mismatch only hits the tail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply an off-the-shelf structured depth-noise simulation to an existing synthetic dataset, retrain, and compare against the clean-depth baseline on a small real set in one day.

one_line_idea: Reconstructing real scenes into neural 3D representations and re-rendering them with perturbed cameras yields dense supervision with real appearance, and this real2sim2real data beats graphics rendering for dense tasks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Neural scene reconstruction methods can rebuild real scenes with photographic appearance and consistent geometry, but dense-task training data is still predominantly produced by classical graphics pipelines with synthetic assets.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-rendered reconstructions of real scenes carry near-zero appearance gap while providing multi-view-consistent depth, correspondence, and segmentation propagation labels, and their geometric imperfections harm dense students less than the appearance gap of classical rendering does.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained on reconstruction-derived data will outperform students trained on equal amounts of classical synthetic data on real evaluations of depth and correspondence, with the advantage growing as evaluation domains approach the reconstructed scene types.
why_important: This replaces the hardest part of synthetic pipelines (making pixels look real) with capture, which scales with commodity cameras rather than artist labor.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Reconstruction-as-data-engine is emerging in robotics, but a head-to-head dense-task comparison against classical synthetic datasets at matched budget may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reconstruct a set of real scenes, generate perturbed-view training data with derived depth and correspondence labels, train students, and compare against classical-synthetic-trained students on real dense benchmarks.
main_risk: Reconstruction failures (floaters, wrong geometry in reflective regions) produce structured label errors concentrated exactly where dense tasks are hardest, potentially poisoning the tail.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic data is mentally equated with graphics assets; reconstruction outputs are viewed as visualization artifacts rather than a labeled-data source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance is the axis models are most sensitive to and reconstruction gets it almost exactly right by construction, while its geometry errors resemble ordinary label noise that training averages over.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use public scene reconstructions to derive depth training pairs for a handful of scenes, fine-tune a small depth model, and compare against fine-tuning on classical synthetic frames of the same count.

one_line_idea: Domain randomization mostly re-implements strong 2D augmentation, and equally aggressive augmentation of a small real set matches heavy randomization in simulation for many perception tasks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Domain randomization varies textures, lighting, and colors in simulation to force invariance, while modern training recipes independently apply strong 2D photometric and geometric augmentation, and the two are rarely compared as substitutes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A large fraction of domain randomization's benefit is expressible as image-space augmentation, so its unique contribution beyond a strong augmentation baseline is limited to 3D-consistent variation (viewpoint, occlusion, geometry) that 2D augmentation cannot mimic.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Ablating domain randomization into its 2D-expressible and 3D-only components will show the 2D-expressible part accounts for the majority of the transfer gain, and a strong-augmentation real-data baseline will close most of the gap attributed to randomization in prior comparisons.
why_important: If randomization is mostly augmentation, simulation infrastructure is being credited for gains obtainable with a data loader, and the honest unique value of simulation is narrower than claimed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Domain randomization papers predate modern augmentation recipes, and a decomposition study under current baselines may not have been redone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with full randomization, with only its 2D-expressible factors applied as augmentation to fixed renders, and with only 3D factors randomized; compare real-data transfer across the three at equal compute.
main_risk: The decomposition into 2D-expressible and 3D-only factors is imperfect because some texture randomization interacts with geometry through shading.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Domain randomization is viewed as a distinct sim-to-real technique whose gains are additional to standard augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance is invariance: the network cannot tell whether color jitter came from a renderer or an augmentation op, so only the 3D-consistent factors can carry unique value.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one published randomization setup, freeze its renders, re-express its photometric factors as augmentations, and compare transfer in two training runs.

one_line_idea: Reported sim-to-real gaps are inflated by label-convention mismatch, and convention-harmonized re-evaluation shrinks the gap across published setups.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sim-to-real gaps are measured by training on synthetic labels and evaluating against real-benchmark labels, silently combining appearance shift with differences in how the two label sources define boundaries, classes, and instances.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A systematic fraction of the measured gap is target-function mismatch from label conventions rather than model failure to generalize over pixels, and this fraction is large enough to change conclusions about adaptation methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating sim-trained models against real labels transformed into the synthetic convention (and vice versa) will produce materially smaller gaps, and part of the ranking among adaptation methods will change because some methods mostly learn the convention rather than the domain.
why_important: The gap number drives the field's research priorities; if a chunk of it is bookkeeping, adaptation methods are being rewarded for convention learning rather than genuine robustness.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Convention mismatch is occasionally noted anecdotally, but a quantified decomposition of the sim-to-real gap into convention and appearance components appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct bidirectional label-convention transforms for one synthetic-real dataset pair, re-evaluate a set of sim-trained and adapted models under harmonized conventions, and report the gap decomposition.
main_risk: Convention transforms cannot be perfect, and residual transform error could be misread as appearance gap or vice versa.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The measured gap is interpreted as purely a generalization failure over image appearance and content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense metrics are exquisitely sensitive to boundary and class-definition choices, and the two label sources were produced by entirely different processes with no shared guideline.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Measure inter-source label disagreement directly by rendering synthetic-style labels for a few real scenes with available 3D reconstructions and computing the metric ceiling this disagreement imposes.

one_line_idea: Foundation-model backbones have made photorealism largely obsolete for sim-to-real: with frozen pretrained features, low-fidelity rendering transfers as well as high-fidelity rendering.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The case for photorealistic simulation was built in the era of training networks from scratch on synthetic data, while modern practice fine-tunes or probes backbones pretrained on web-scale real imagery.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pretrained backbones already map low-fidelity and high-fidelity renders of the same content to nearby features, so the marginal transfer value of photorealism collapses once a strong pretrained backbone is used, surviving only for from-scratch training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A rendering-fidelity sweep crossed with backbone initialization (scratch versus pretrained-frozen versus pretrained-finetuned) will show a strong fidelity effect for scratch training and a near-flat fidelity curve for pretrained backbones on real-data evaluation.
why_important: Photorealism is the single most expensive line item in synthetic pipelines; if pretrained backbones neutralize it, budgets should shift to content diversity and label quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both fidelity studies and pretrained-backbone studies exist separately, but the interaction claim (pretraining eliminates the fidelity effect) may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one scene corpus at multiple fidelity levels, train dense heads under the three initialization regimes, and evaluate transfer on real benchmarks; the interaction term is the result.
main_risk: Fidelity levels are hard to vary cleanly without also varying content visibility (shadows revealing geometry), which can contaminate the sweep.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Higher rendering fidelity is assumed to monotonically improve sim-to-real transfer regardless of the training recipe.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The invariances that photorealism buys were already learned by the backbone from billions of real images, so paying for them again in the renderer purchases nothing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a pretrained backbone versus a scratch model on an existing low-fidelity synthetic dataset and compare how much of the gap to a high-fidelity dataset remains in each regime.

one_line_idea: The direction and size of the sim-real transfer asymmetry (sim-to-real versus real-to-sim) is a cheap diagnostic that identifies whether a gap is appearance-driven or content-driven.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Sim-to-real transfer is measured in one direction; the reverse direction (train real, test synthetic) is almost never reported, discarding half of the available signal about what the gap consists of.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Appearance-driven gaps produce roughly symmetric bidirectional degradation, while content-coverage gaps produce asymmetric degradation (the side with narrower content transfers worse outward), so the asymmetry profile classifies gap type without any adaptation experiments.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across multiple synthetic-real dataset pairs, pairs known for narrow synthetic content will show strong asymmetry, pairs with matched content but different rendering will show near-symmetric gaps, and the asymmetry measure will predict which adaptation family (appearance translation versus content resampling) helps more.
why_important: Teams currently choose adaptation methods by trial and error; a two-evaluation diagnostic that predicts the right intervention family would save large amounts of engineering.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bidirectional evaluation appears occasionally as a curiosity, but its use as a systematic gap-type diagnostic with validated predictions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several dataset pairs, train models in both directions, compute the asymmetry index, then run one appearance-level and one content-level adaptation per pair and test whether the index predicts which one wins.
main_risk: Dataset difficulty differences (one side simply harder) also produce asymmetry and must be normalized out with within-domain baselines.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The gap is treated as a scalar property of the pair, and the reverse direction is considered uninformative because nobody deploys on synthetic data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer asymmetry is exactly the fingerprint of support mismatch in distribution shift, and support mismatch (content) versus density mismatch (appearance) is the decision-relevant distinction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick two dataset pairs with opposite expected profiles, run the four training jobs, and check whether the asymmetry ordering matches expectation.

one_line_idea: Models exploit renderer-specific spectral and noise signatures as shortcuts, and matching low-level image statistics between synthetic and real data removes a large, cheap-to-fix share of the sim-to-real gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rendered images differ from camera images in high-frequency statistics: absence of sensor noise, different demosaicing, sharper anti-aliased edges, and characteristic tone mapping, and networks are known to be sensitive to such low-level regularities.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A significant portion of the sim-to-real appearance gap lives in these camera-pipeline statistics rather than in scene realism, so passing synthetic images through a calibrated camera-pipeline simulation (noise, optics blur, compression) recovers much of the gap at negligible cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Adding a physically motivated camera-pipeline simulation to synthetic training images will improve real-data performance across several dense tasks, and the improvement will overlap substantially with what expensive photorealism upgrades deliver, indicating a shared mechanism.
why_important: Camera-pipeline simulation is a few lines of differentiable image processing, while photorealism costs artist and compute budgets; establishing equivalence would deflate the realism requirement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual pieces (noise augmentation, ISP simulation) exist, but positioning the camera pipeline as the dominant appearance-gap channel with an overlap analysis against realism upgrades may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on synthetic data with and without calibrated ISP simulation, compare against a higher-fidelity render of the same content, and measure how much of the fidelity gain the ISP simulation alone reproduces.
main_risk: ISP parameters vary across target cameras, and a single calibration may under-represent the achievable gain or overfit one device.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The appearance gap is attributed to scene-level realism (materials, lighting, geometry detail) rather than to the capture pipeline.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks latch onto the most reliable discriminative statistics available, and pipeline signatures are globally present in every pixel of every frame, making them the easiest shortcut to learn and the most damaging mismatch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small synthetic-versus-real domain classifier, ablate its input to high-frequency residuals only, and check whether domain discrimination survives; if it does, pipeline statistics carry the domain signal.

one_line_idea: Sim-to-real adaptation method rankings established on driving benchmarks do not transfer to other target domains, making the canonical leaderboard a domain artifact.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The dominant sim-to-real benchmarks in segmentation are synthetic-driving to real-driving transfers, and most adaptation methods are developed and ranked exclusively in that setting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Adaptation methods encode driving-specific inductive bets (sky-road layout priors, class frequency structure, urban texture statistics), so their relative ranking changes substantially when the same protocol is applied to indoor, agricultural, industrial, or aerial synthetic-real pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running a set of published adaptation methods across several non-driving synthetic-real pairs will yield rank correlations with the driving leaderboard substantially below 1, with some methods dropping from top to bottom quartile.
why_important: Practitioners in non-driving domains select methods from driving leaderboards; if rankings do not transfer, those selections are close to arbitrary.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cross-dataset checks exist within driving, but a systematic cross-domain re-ranking study of sim-to-real methods may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix architecture and training budget, run several representative adaptation methods on three or more synthetic-real pairs from distinct domains, and report the rank stability across pairs.
main_risk: Method implementations are tuned to their original benchmarks, and honest re-tuning per domain is expensive but necessary for a fair ranking.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A method that wins on the canonical driving transfers is assumed to be a generally better sim-to-real method.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptation methods rely on unlabeled target statistics whose structure differs radically across domains, so there is no a priori reason for rank stability, and the field simply has not measured it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take three adaptation methods with public code and one non-driving synthetic-real pair, run them at default settings, and check whether the driving ordering is preserved.

one_line_idea: Adapting label-space statistics (class frequencies, object size and count distributions) via resampling beats image-space adaptation for sim-to-real transfer at a fraction of the cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets have class balance, object density, and size distributions chosen by generator authors, which typically diverge from real benchmark statistics; adaptation research nonetheless focuses on translating pixels rather than reshaping these label-space distributions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A meaningful share of the sim-to-real gap is prior mismatch in label-space statistics, so importance resampling of synthetic data to match target label statistics (estimated from limited target metadata or pseudo-labels) delivers gains competitive with image translation methods.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At equal compute, label-statistics resampling of a synthetic dataset will match or exceed a representative image-translation baseline on real evaluation, and the two will combine additively, indicating they address different gap components.
why_important: Resampling is free at training time and reusable across architectures, whereas translation networks are expensive, fragile, and can corrupt labels.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-balancing tricks are folklore, but framing label-space statistics matching as a complete adaptation method benchmarked against image translation may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate target label statistics from a small real validation set, resample the synthetic training set to match, train identically, and compare against an image-translation pipeline and their combination.
main_risk: Aggressive resampling reduces effective dataset size, and the diversity loss could offset the prior-matching gain at small synthetic pool sizes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The sim-to-real gap is seen as an appearance problem to be fixed in pixel space, with dataset statistics treated as a fixed property of the source data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense predictors internalize label priors strongly (frequency, scale, and co-occurrence), so shipping the wrong priors may be as damaging as shipping the wrong textures, yet is far easier to fix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Reweight one synthetic dataset to the target class-frequency histogram, retrain one model, and compare against the unweighted baseline on real validation in a single day.

one_line_idea: For contact-rich robotic perception, physics fidelity dominates visual fidelity in sim-to-real transfer, inverting the effort allocation of typical simulation pipelines.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Simulation pipelines for robot perception invest heavily in visual realism, while contact physics (deformation, friction-driven pose outcomes, settling configurations) is approximated crudely; perception models consume images whose content is generated by that physics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For tasks whose labels depend on physically plausible object configurations (grasp points, stable poses, cluttered pile perception), errors in physics generate systematically wrong scene content, and this content error transfers worse than rendering error of equal apparent magnitude.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Crossing physics fidelity with visual fidelity in a grasp-perception or pile-segmentation setup will show a larger real-world performance effect from physics fidelity, and errors of physics-poor models will concentrate on configuration-dependent predictions rather than appearance-dependent ones.
why_important: Physics and rendering budgets compete in every robotics simulation stack, and the field lacks controlled evidence about which purchase matters for perception (as opposed to control).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Physics fidelity is studied for policy learning, but its isolated effect on perception transfer with rendering held fixed may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate cluttered-scene datasets under two physics settings (fast approximate versus accurate) and two rendering settings, train perception models in all four cells, and evaluate on real cluttered scenes.
main_risk: Accurate physics changes the visual distribution too (different piles look different), so attribution requires careful matched-content controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Visual realism is assumed to be the binding constraint for perception transfer, with physics mattering only for control policies.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A perceptually perfect render of a physically impossible pile teaches the model a world that does not exist, and content-level lies are harder to unlearn than texture-level ones.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare real-world detection of stably-resting objects between models trained on physics-settled versus pose-randomized synthetic scenes at identical rendering, in two runs.

one_line_idea: A large share of the sim-to-real gap lives in normalization statistics, and recalibrating them with a handful of unlabeled real images recovers it without touching any weights.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Networks trained on synthetic data carry normalization statistics and activation distributions fitted to rendered inputs, and test-time normalization adaptation is a known cheap trick in the corruption-robustness literature that is rarely positioned as a sim-to-real baseline.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For sim-trained dense models, recomputing normalization statistics on a small unlabeled real sample captures a disproportionate share of what full unsupervised domain adaptation achieves, implying much of the gap is a first-order input-distribution shift rather than a representational deficiency.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Normalization-statistic adaptation with tens to hundreds of unlabeled real images will recover a substantial fraction of the gap closed by full adaptation methods across several synthetic-real pairs, and published adaptation gains will shrink notably when this baseline is included.
why_important: If a zero-training baseline captures much of the reported adaptation gain, the effective novelty of many adaptation methods is smaller than presented, and practitioners get most of the value for free.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Normalization adaptation is known for corruption robustness, but its systematic use as a mandatory sim-to-real baseline with gap-decomposition framing may be absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several sim-trained models, apply normalization recalibration on small real samples, measure recovered performance, and compare against published full-adaptation results under identical evaluation.
main_risk: Architectures without batch-statistic normalization layers weaken the intervention, so the claim may be architecture-dependent and needs a modern normalization-free control.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The sim-to-real gap is assumed to require substantial adaptation machinery or retraining to address.
why_it_might_be_wrong: First-moment and second-moment input shifts are exactly what normalization layers absorb, and rendered-to-real is plausibly dominated by such low-order shifts once content overlaps.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one public sim-trained segmentation model, recompute its normalization statistics on unlabeled real frames, and re-evaluate; an hour-scale experiment.

one_line_idea: Generative image translation of synthetic frames corrupts dense labels by hallucinating and deleting content, so translation-based sim-to-real gains are overstated for dense tasks and label-corruption audits should be mandatory.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A standard sim-to-real recipe translates synthetic images toward real appearance with generative models while reusing the original synthetic labels, assuming the translation preserves content alignment with the labels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Translation networks alter content at a non-trivial rate (removing thin structures, hallucinating textures over small objects, shifting boundaries), so the effective training set has systematically corrupted labels, and part of the reported gains would grow if corruption were measured and filtered.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An audit that measures label-image consistency before and after translation will find systematic content drift concentrated on small objects and thin structures, and filtering or re-labeling drifted regions will improve final transfer beyond the unfiltered translation pipeline.
why_important: Translation pipelines are widely deployed; if they quietly poison dense labels, the field is both under-measuring their harm and leaving an easy improvement (drift filtering) on the table.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Content-preservation losses exist in translation methods, but a quantitative label-corruption audit tied to downstream dense-task impact may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a standard translation pipeline, quantify per-pixel content drift with the source labels and a consistency detector, train students on unfiltered versus drift-filtered translated data, and compare real-data results.
main_risk: Consistency detection itself uses a model that may share blind spots with the translator, underestimating drift on exactly the affected regions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Translation is assumed approximately content-preserving, and its gains are attributed entirely to appearance alignment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generative translators optimize distribution-level realism with weak instance-level constraints, and small objects are statistically cheap to delete, exactly where dense metrics are most sensitive.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Overlay original masks on translated frames for a random sample and manually count label-content mismatches on small objects; a one-afternoon audit that establishes whether the corruption rate is non-trivial.

one_line_idea: The sim-to-real gap follows its own scaling law with synthetic dataset size, and the exponent difference against real-data scaling predicts crossover budgets where adding synthetic stops helping.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scaling laws are established for model and data size within a distribution, but sim-to-real practice lacks quantitative guidance for how transfer performance scales as synthetic data grows and where it saturates relative to adding real data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Real-test error of sim-trained models follows a power-law-plus-floor in synthetic dataset size, with the floor set by the domain gap; jointly fitting synthetic and real scaling curves yields a predictable crossover budget beyond which synthetic marginal value collapses.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across several synthetic-real pairs and tasks, small-scale pilot fits of the two-curve model will predict large-scale mixed-data outcomes within useful tolerance, including the observed saturation point of synthetic additions.
why_important: Teams currently guess synthetic volumes; a fitted gap-scaling law converts pilot runs into quantitative generation-budget decisions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Scaling analyses of transfer exist, but a validated gap-floor scaling law used prescriptively for synthetic budget planning may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train models on nested synthetic subsets and nested real subsets, fit the two-term scaling model, predict mixed-budget outcomes, and verify with held-out large-budget runs.
main_risk: The floor may drift with dataset composition rather than staying constant, breaking the simple functional form and requiring composition-aware extensions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] More synthetic data is assumed to be monotonically better, or dismissed wholesale, with little quantitative interpolation between the two attitudes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Within-distribution scaling laws are among the most reproducible empirical results in deep learning, and there is no obvious reason transfer curves would resist the same treatment.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit the model on one dataset pair with five subset sizes and check the predicted saturation against one larger run; roughly a week of scheduled small trainings.

one_line_idea: Weather and lighting randomization in driving simulation covers a thin manifold of real conditions, and a nearest-neighbor coverage audit predicts per-condition transfer failure before any training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Driving simulators expose a handful of parametric weather presets, while real conditions form a high-dimensional continuum of illumination, precipitation, optics effects, and sensor responses; coverage of that continuum is asserted rather than measured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The per-condition transfer performance of sim-trained models is predictable from a coverage measure (distance from each real condition to its nearest synthetic neighbor in a perceptual feature space), making condition-coverage auditing a pre-training diagnostic.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Stratifying real evaluation data by nearest-synthetic-neighbor distance will show monotonically degrading performance with distance, and expanding simulation coverage specifically in high-distance regions will yield larger gains than uniform data additions.
why_important: Safety cases for simulation-trained driving systems rest on coverage claims; a validated audit converts those claims from marketing into measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Feature-space domain distance measures exist, but validating condition-level coverage distance as a predictor of stratified transfer failure in driving may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Embed synthetic and real frames with a fixed pretrained encoder, compute per-real-frame coverage distances, evaluate a sim-trained model stratified by distance, and test targeted coverage expansion against uniform expansion.
main_risk: The pretrained embedding may compress away condition factors that matter to the task, weakening the distance-performance correlation for spurious reasons.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Enumerating named weather presets is treated as sufficient evidence of condition coverage in simulation-based validation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer failure is fundamentally a support problem, and nearest-neighbor distance in an appropriate space is the most direct measurable proxy for being off-support.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute coverage distances for an existing sim-trained model's evaluation set and check the distance-versus-error correlation with no new training at all.

one_line_idea: Pixel-perfect synthetic labels can transfer worse than convention-matched noisy labels because evaluation rewards agreement with human annotator behavior, not with geometric truth.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real benchmarks are labeled by humans whose systematic imprecision and conventions define the scoring target, while synthetic data supplies geometrically exact labels; the two notions of ground truth silently differ.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When evaluation labels contain systematic human bias, training on exact synthetic labels optimizes a subtly different target, so injecting human-like structured noise into synthetic labels improves benchmark scores even though it degrades geometric truthfulness.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A human-annotation-noise model fitted from real double-annotated data, applied to synthetic labels, will improve real-benchmark scores of synthetic-trained models relative to exact labels, with gains concentrated where annotator bias is largest (boundaries, thin parts, ambiguous classes).
why_important: This exposes a perverse property of current benchmarks (rewarding replication of annotator bias) and gives synthetic-data users an immediate lever; it also argues for truth-calibrated evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label-noise simulation is usually studied as a harm; using fitted annotator-noise models as a transfer-improving alignment step for synthetic data may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a structured annotator-noise model from a doubly annotated real subset, apply it to synthetic training labels, train matched models on exact versus noise-aligned labels, and compare on the real benchmark plus a geometric-truth proxy.
main_risk: If benchmark annotation bias is small or heterogeneous across annotators, the fitted noise model adds variance without a systematic target to align to.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Cleaner labels are assumed to be strictly better training signal, making pixel-perfect synthetic labels an unquestioned advantage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Supervised learning optimizes agreement with the evaluation distribution, and if that distribution is biased, matching the bias is what scores; truth is not the target the metric measures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply simple boundary erosion and dilation mimicking known annotator tendencies to synthetic masks, retrain quickly, and check the direction of the benchmark-score change.

one_line_idea: Foundation-model pseudo-labels carry attribute-correlated structured noise, so noise-robust learning methods validated on uniform synthetic noise fail on the auto-label noise that actually matters now.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The learning-with-noisy-labels literature validates methods predominantly with synthetic uniform or class-conditional flips injected into clean datasets, while modern datasets are increasingly labeled by foundation models whose errors correlate with visual attributes, rarity, and ambiguity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Methods that win under injected-flip noise rely on assumptions (noise independent of input given class) violated by model-generated noise, so their ranking collapses or inverts under real auto-label noise.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Benchmarking representative noise-robust methods on datasets labeled by actual foundation-model annotators (with verified clean evaluation labels) will produce method rankings with low rank correlation to the injected-noise leaderboard, and simple baselines will close most of the claimed gaps.
why_important: Auto-labeling is becoming the dominant labeling mode; if the field's noise-robustness toolkit is validated against the wrong noise family, practitioners are importing false confidence into production pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Instance-dependent noise is studied abstractly, but a benchmark built from genuine foundation-model annotator errors with method re-ranking may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Auto-label several datasets with public foundation models, keep human-verified evaluation splits, run the standard noise-robust method suite, and compare rankings against the injected-noise setting on the same datasets.
main_risk: Verified-clean evaluation labels are expensive, and residual evaluation noise could blur method differences.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Noise-robust methods are assumed to generalize across noise families, and injected-flip validation is treated as sufficient evidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model-generated errors are confidently wrong on systematic input regions, the exact regime where small-loss and disagreement heuristics break, because the noisy label looks self-consistent.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Auto-label one mid-sized dataset, run two flagship noise-robust methods plus a plain baseline, and check whether the flagship advantage survives; a few GPU-days.

one_line_idea: Synthetic recaptioning of image-text data injects the captioner's systematic biases, and students trained on recaptioned corpora inherit a measurable error fingerprint from the captioning model.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large image-text training corpora are increasingly rewritten by captioning models to improve text quality, replacing noisy-but-independent alt-text with fluent captions generated by a single model family.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Recaptioning trades independent random noise for correlated systematic noise (hallucinated attributes, template phrasings, coverage blind spots), and students trained on recaptioned data reproduce the captioner's specific error pattern, detectable as fingerprint inheritance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained on corpora recaptioned by different captioners will exhibit error profiles that cluster by captioner identity rather than by student architecture, and attribute-hallucination probes will show statistically matched failure signatures between each student and its captioner.
why_important: If error fingerprints propagate, single-captioner recaptioning creates a monoculture where independent models share failure modes, undermining ensemble safety arguments and evaluation independence.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Recaptioning quality gains are documented, but systematic inheritance of captioner-specific errors by downstream students may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recaption one corpus with two different captioners, train matched students on each, build an attribute-level error probe suite, and test whether student errors cluster by captioner.
main_risk: Disentangling captioner fingerprints from shared dataset effects requires the same underlying images across conditions, which constrains corpus scale.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Recaptioning is viewed as strictly improving label quality, with its noise treated as reduced rather than restructured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Independent noise averages out under scale while correlated noise does not; replacing the former with the latter can be a net harm precisely in the large-data regime where averaging was the safety mechanism.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe an existing pair of public models known to be trained with and without recaptioned data on a small hallucination-sensitive test and compare error-pattern similarity to the captioner's own errors.

one_line_idea: Boundary-localized label noise damages segmentation training far more per pixel than interior noise, and a boundary-weighted noise metric predicts downstream harm where raw noise rate fails.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Label noise in dense annotation is summarized as a scalar corrupted-pixel rate, treating all pixels equally, while gradients near boundaries dominate what segmentation networks learn about shape.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The damage function of dense label noise is strongly spatially non-uniform, concentrated in boundary bands, so two datasets with equal noise rates can differ widely in training value, and a boundary-weighted noise measure recovers the missing predictive power.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlled corruption experiments placing equal pixel budgets of noise in boundary bands versus interiors will show substantially larger degradation for boundary placement, and the proposed weighted metric will predict final model quality across mixed-noise datasets better than raw noise rate.
why_important: Annotation-budget and cleaning decisions currently optimize raw error rates; spatial weighting would redirect cleaning effort to where it changes model quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary sensitivity is folklore in segmentation, but a validated spatially weighted noise metric with predictive evaluation may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Corrupt clean synthetic labels with spatially controlled noise at matched budgets, train matched models per condition, and regress final performance on candidate noise metrics.
main_risk: The optimal spatial weighting likely depends on architecture and loss, so the metric may need per-family calibration to stay predictive.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense label quality is communicated and contracted as an overall pixel accuracy percentage.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Losses and metrics are disproportionately influenced by boundary regions, and interior pixels are largely redundant given surrounding context, making uniform pixel accounting a poor model of information content.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two corruption conditions, two short trainings on one dataset; the effect direction is checkable within a day.

one_line_idea: Auto-label noise correlates with example difficulty, so confidence-based label cleaning preferentially deletes hard examples and produces models that score better on clean averages but worse on hard tails.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Data-cleaning pipelines flag samples where labels disagree with model predictions or have low confidence, and auto-generated labels are least reliable exactly on visually difficult examples.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because label error and example difficulty are confounded in auto-labeled data, cleaning removes a difficulty-biased subset, silently shifting the training distribution toward easy content and degrading tail robustness even as headline metrics improve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing cleaned versus uncleaned auto-labeled training with difficulty-stratified evaluation will show cleaning improves average metrics while degrading the hardest strata, and a difficulty-controlled cleaning method (re-labeling instead of deleting hard samples) will beat both.
why_important: Cleaning is universally recommended; if it trades tail performance for average performance, deployed models inherit hidden fragility in exactly the cases that matter for safety.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Difficulty-noise confounding is acknowledged conceptually, but a stratified demonstration that standard cleaning harms tails, plus a re-label-not-delete remedy, may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Auto-label a dataset, apply standard confidence-based cleaning, train on cleaned and raw versions, and evaluate on difficulty-stratified real test data, then add a targeted re-labeling arm for flagged-hard samples.
main_risk: Difficulty stratification itself relies on a model or heuristic, and a poorly chosen difficulty proxy could manufacture or hide the effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Removing suspicious labels is assumed to be conservative and safe, with the removed mass treated as noise rather than signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In auto-labeled data the flag for wrong label and the flag for informative example are the same flag, so deletion implements inverse-difficulty sampling, the opposite of curriculum wisdom.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Rank a cleaned-out subset by a difficulty proxy and simply inspect whether removed examples skew hard; if not, the confounding premise dies before any training.

one_line_idea: The learning-with-noisy-labels leaderboard is a simulation artifact: method rankings under injected noise do not survive on datasets whose noise arose organically from real annotation processes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks in noisy-label learning largely inject synthetic flips into clean datasets because organic-noise datasets with verified clean test labels are scarce, and methods are ranked on the injected settings.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Organic annotation noise (guideline ambiguity, attention lapses, systematic misreading of certain classes) has statistical structure absent from injected flips, so a substantial fraction of reported method-over-baseline gains are artifacts of the injection procedure.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On datasets with organically noisy training labels and independently verified test labels, published gaps between flagship noise-robust methods and simple baselines (loss clipping, early stopping, mixup-style regularization) will shrink substantially, and rankings will reorder.
why_important: The field ships methods to practitioners based on these leaderboards; a re-grounding on organic noise either validates or deflates a decade of methodology.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Some organic-noise datasets exist, but a comprehensive re-ranking study framed as an injection-artifact audit may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble several organically noisy training sets with verified evaluation labels across task types, run the standard method suite with equalized tuning budgets, and compare gaps and rankings against the injected-noise versions of the same data.
main_risk: Organic noise rates are unknown and heterogeneous, complicating like-for-like comparison with controlled injection levels.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Injected-noise benchmarks are treated as adequate proxies, and method gains are assumed to transfer to real noisy data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Methods co-evolved with the injection procedure for years, a classic setup for benchmark overfitting to a noise family nobody encounters in practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pick one organically noisy dataset, run three flagship methods and two trivial baselines, and check whether the leaderboard gap reproduces.

one_line_idea: Ensembling multiple foundation-model teachers barely reduces auto-label noise because their errors are correlated through shared pretraining data, violating the independence assumption behind ensemble labeling.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A standard remedy for auto-label noise is aggregating labels from multiple teacher models, borrowing the logic of annotator aggregation which assumes substantially independent errors, while modern foundation models overlap heavily in web-scale training data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-teacher error correlation on auto-labeling tasks is high enough that aggregation yields far less noise reduction than the independent-error model predicts, and the residual shared errors are systematic (rare classes, ambiguous viewpoints) rather than random.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring pairwise error correlation among diverse public teachers on verified evaluation sets will reveal substantial positive correlation, and students trained on aggregated labels will improve only marginally over the best single teacher, far below the independence-predicted gain.
