community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generation-for-data means producing images; labels are assumed to be the thing synthetic pipelines get for free and real data lacks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Students are more robust to label noise than to input distribution shift, so putting the noise on the label side of the training pair is the better side of the trade.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one segmentation dataset, compare a student trained on extraction-derived masks over real images against one trained on an existing synthetic dataset of matched size; two runs decide the direction.

one_line_idea: Published diffusion-augmentation gains shrink dramatically against modern strong-augmentation baselines, surviving mainly in low-data regimes, and a reproduction matrix would recalibrate the field's expectations.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many papers report classifier and detector improvements from adding diffusion-generated images, but baseline augmentation recipes vary widely across these papers and are often weaker than current best practice.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial portion of reported generative-augmentation gains duplicates what strong conventional augmentation already provides, so under equalized modern baselines the marginal gain concentrates in genuinely low-data regimes and vanishes at scale.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running representative generative-augmentation setups across a data-volume ladder with strong and weak conventional-augmentation baselines will show the generative gain shrinking as baseline strength and data volume grow, with an interaction pattern consistent with mechanism overlap.
why_important: Generation is orders of magnitude costlier than augmentation ops; if the gains overlap, cost-benefit analyses in industry are being made on inflated numbers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual comparisons exist; a systematic equal-baseline reproduction matrix across regimes may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select several published generative-augmentation configurations, re-run each under weak and strong conventional baselines at several real-data volumes, and report the gain surface.
main_risk: Faithful reproduction of published setups is laborious, and deviations could be blamed for any shrinkage found.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generative augmentation is assumed to add value on top of any conventional recipe because it injects semantic novelty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Much of what generated images add (photometric variety, texture variation, pose jitter) is exactly what strong augmentation manufactures for free, so the two interventions plausibly compete for the same headroom.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One dataset, one generative-augmentation recipe, crossed with weak versus strong baseline augmentation; four runs reveal whether the generative gain survives the strong baseline.

one_line_idea: Students inherit compositional failure modes of their generative teachers: training on diffusion data measurably degrades counting and structural accuracy relative to matched real-data training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text-to-image generators systematically fail at object counts, structural details, and text rendering, and their outputs increasingly enter training corpora for downstream vision models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These structured failures act as systematic label-free noise in the image distribution, so students trained on generated data develop corresponding deficits (counting, part-structure, text-in-image reading) even when their aggregate accuracy matches real-trained students.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Matching real-trained and synthetic-trained students on aggregate benchmarks and then probing with counting, part-consistency, and text-reading suites will reveal selective deficits in the synthetic-trained students aligned with the teacher generator's documented failure categories.
why_important: Aggregate-matched models are treated as interchangeable; selective structural deficits would mean synthetic-trained models carry hidden weaknesses exactly where generators are known to fail.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Generator failures are documented at the image level; their inheritance as selective student deficits may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched students on real versus generated corpora to equal aggregate performance, then evaluate on a targeted probe battery covering known generator failure categories, comparing deficit profiles.
main_risk: Achieving aggregate-matched students requires careful budget tuning, and mismatch would confound the selective-deficit reading.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] If a synthetic-trained model matches benchmarks, its training data provenance is assumed not to matter.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training data defines the world model; a world where object counts are unreliable teaches a student that counts are unreliable, and no aggregate metric is sensitive enough to notice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe two existing public models with known real-versus-synthetic-heavy training recipes on a counting suite; a suggestive deficit pattern justifies the controlled study.

one_line_idea: Web-crawl vintages carry rising synthetic fractions, and models pretrained on different crawl vintages show behavior drift attributable to synthetic contamination, making vintage a measurable data-quality variable.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The public web increasingly contains generated imagery, so crawls from different years embed different synthetic fractions, yet pretraining corpora are versioned by size and source, not by synthetic contamination level.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Synthetic fraction is a systematic function of crawl date, and models pretrained on later vintages exhibit measurable behavioral shifts (texture statistics preferences, structural-detail handling, robustness profile changes) that track the contamination level rather than content drift alone.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Controlling content topics while varying crawl vintage will still produce student behavior differences correlated with independently estimated synthetic fractions, and spiking older corpora with known synthetic content will reproduce the same drift signature.
why_important: If vintage effects are real, reproducibility and model comparisons across years are silently confounded, and data pipelines need contamination accounting the way they need dedup today.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Synthetic-content growth is documented; its causal footprint on pretrained-model behavior across crawl vintages may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble topic-matched corpora from different crawl vintages, estimate synthetic fractions with detectors, pretrain matched models, and compare behavior probes, validating causality with synthetic-spiking controls.
main_risk: Synthetic-content detectors are imperfect and their errors correlate with time, threatening the fraction estimates the analysis rests on.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Crawl date is treated as affecting content freshness, not data authenticity, in corpus construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contamination is monotone in time and mechanically enters every undated pipeline, so its effects must surface somewhere; the only question is detectability, which the spiking control answers.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a synthetic-content detector over two crawl vintages to verify the fraction gradient exists at meaningful magnitude before committing to any pretraining runs.

one_line_idea: Bilevel-optimal data generation (generate to directly maximize student validation improvement) is approximable by first-order gradient matching at a tiny fraction of the cost, capturing most of its gain.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic training data is generated by prompt heuristics that never see the student's actual needs, while the true objective (generate data that maximally improves the student on a validation distribution) is a bilevel problem considered computationally prohibitive.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The bilevel objective's value is dominated by its first-order component (generating samples whose training gradients align with the student's validation-loss gradient), so a cheap gradient-matching guidance signal on the generator captures most of the bilevel gain without inner-loop retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Gradient-matched generation will outperform prompt-heuristic generation at matched budgets on student validation metrics, and a small-scale exact-bilevel comparison will show the first-order approximation recovering a large fraction of the exact method's improvement.
why_important: Closing the loop between student needs and data generation is the natural endpoint of data-centric AI; a tractable approximation would make it deployable rather than theoretical.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-matching appears in dataset distillation; using it as generation guidance for large generative models in a student-aware loop may be unexplored at practical scale.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement gradient-matching guidance for a conditional generator, compare student outcomes against heuristic generation at matched budgets, and validate the approximation quality against exact bilevel optimization in a deliberately small setting.
main_risk: Gradient signals from the student may drive the generator off its reliable manifold, producing adversarial-looking samples that game the first-order objective without helping actual training.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Student-aware generation is assumed to require intractable nested optimization, so pipelines settle for student-blind heuristics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most of the benefit of targeting plausibly lives in coarse direction (which regions of data space help now), which first-order signals capture, rather than in the fine structure only exact bilevel sees.
fastest_falsification_experiment: In a small classification setting, compare heuristic versus gradient-matched generation for one student over one round; the ordering plus an exact-bilevel anchor is computable in days.

one_line_idea: Deliberately generating realistic near-miss hard negatives improves fine-grained discrimination more than generating additional positives, making negative synthesis the underused half of generative augmentation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Generative augmentation overwhelmingly produces positive examples of target classes, while discriminative errors concentrate on confusable near-misses, which real datasets undersample and generators are rarely asked to produce.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generators can be steered to produce calibrated near-miss negatives (almost-correct examples crossing a decision boundary), and at matched budgets such negatives sharpen decision boundaries more than additional positives, especially for fine-grained and safety-relevant distinctions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Augmenting with generated near-miss negatives will outperform augmenting with the same count of generated positives on fine-grained discrimination metrics and reduce specific confusion-pair error rates, with gains concentrated on the targeted boundaries.
why_important: Boundary sharpness is what deployment errors are made of; a systematic negative-synthesis methodology would attack errors where they live instead of reinforcing already-learned regions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Hard-negative mining exists for retrieval; systematic generative synthesis of near-miss negatives with boundary-calibration control may be new for visual classification and detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define confusion pairs from a baseline model's errors, generate near-miss negatives per pair via controlled interpolation prompts or attribute edits, retrain with negatives versus positives at matched budgets, and compare pair-level and aggregate metrics.
main_risk: Near-miss generation may cross the boundary unintentionally (producing actual positives labeled negative), injecting exactly the label noise that hurts boundaries most.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generative augmentation means making more examples of what you want to detect, with negatives treated as free background.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decision boundaries are determined by the closest examples on both sides, and the side generators are never asked to populate is the side that limits performance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one known confusion pair, generate near-miss negatives with attribute edits, retrain briefly, and check whether the specific pair confusion drops more than under positive augmentation.

one_line_idea: Generated video is a poor training source for temporal representations because its artifacts are temporal, and hybrid data (generated appearance with real motion) beats end-to-end video generation for training video models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Video generators produce visually appealing frames but exhibit temporal artifacts (identity drift, physics violations, motion discontinuities), and generated video is increasingly proposed as training data for video understanding models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because the artifact budget of video generation concentrates in temporal structure, students trained on generated video learn degenerate temporal features, and composing real motion sources (real videos, motion capture, flow fields) with generated appearance yields strictly better temporal representation learning at matched budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained on fully generated video will underperform hybrid-data students on motion-sensitive evaluations (action granularity, temporal ordering, physics plausibility judgments) while matching them on appearance-sensitive evaluations.
why_important: Video data is the next frontier of synthetic training data, and the naive path (generate videos end-to-end) may be structurally the wrong allocation of generation effort.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Video-generation quality is widely assessed for viewing, but its specific inadequacy as temporal training signal, with a hybrid remedy, may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct matched corpora (fully generated video versus generated-appearance-real-motion hybrids), pretrain matched video models, and evaluate on a battery separating temporal from appearance competence.
main_risk: Hybrid construction pipelines add their own artifacts (warping errors), which could contaminate the comparison unless artifact rates are audited on both arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] As video generators improve visually, their outputs are assumed to become correspondingly good training data for video understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visual quality metrics reward per-frame appearance, which is precisely the component video models can already get elsewhere; the component training needs most (honest temporal structure) is the one generation gets wrong.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe a model pretrained on generated video versus one pretrained on real video with a temporal-order-sensitivity test at matched appearance performance; the selective deficit is checkable with public checkpoints if available.

one_line_idea: Transfer from graphics data scales with distinct 3D asset count without saturating, while realism knobs saturate early, so generation budgets should buy assets, not rendering quality.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Graphics-based dataset budgets are split between asset acquisition and rendering quality, and this allocation is decided by intuition because the marginal returns of each axis have not been measured jointly.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream transfer follows a slowly decaying power law in unique asset count (each new asset adds instance-level variety models still need) but saturates quickly in rendering-quality improvements, so the asset axis dominates at every realistic budget.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A joint sweep over asset count and rendering fidelity at matched total cost will show iso-performance contours running nearly parallel to the fidelity axis beyond a low fidelity threshold, with asset count driving performance throughout the range.
why_important: Asset libraries and render farms are the two big cost centers of simulation pipelines; a measured returns curve would redirect real money.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both axes have been varied separately in dataset papers; a cost-normalized joint returns surface may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: With one procedural pipeline, generate datasets across an asset-count-by-fidelity grid, train matched detection and segmentation models, and map the performance surface against generation cost.
main_risk: Asset quality varies with library size (marginal assets may be worse), confounding count with quality unless assets are randomly subsampled from a fixed pool.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Rendering realism is treated as the prestige axis of simulation quality, with asset variety as a logistics detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Instance diversity is the raw material of category learning, while fidelity beyond a threshold only polishes statistics the backbone already tolerates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Subsample one asset library at two sizes and render at two fidelity levels (four cheap datasets); the relative slopes are visible from four training runs.

one_line_idea: A procedurally infinite stream of moderate-quality scenes beats any fixed-size high-quality synthetic dataset for dense tasks, because non-repetition eliminates the synthetic-overfitting failure mode.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets are shipped as fixed collections that models revisit for many epochs, allowing memorization of specific scenes and renderer quirks, while procedural pipelines could instead generate every training batch fresh.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For matched total training compute, never-repeating procedural streams produce better real-data transfer than fixed datasets of any practical size, because epoch-repetition on synthetic data specifically amplifies renderer-artifact overfitting.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training on a fresh-every-batch stream will outperform training on fixed datasets across sizes at matched compute, and the fixed-dataset deficit will correlate with measures of artifact memorization (train-synthetic versus real-transfer divergence).
why_important: The result would change synthetic data from a dataset product into a generator product, with implications for how synthetic data is packaged, sold, and consumed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Infinite-data training is standard in some simulation domains; a controlled fixed-versus-stream comparison isolating the artifact-overfitting mechanism for dense vision tasks may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a procedural generator and training compute, train models on fixed datasets of several sizes versus a non-repeating stream, and compare real-data transfer plus artifact-memorization diagnostics.
main_risk: Online generation throughput may bottleneck training, and any quality reduction made for speed would confound the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dataset size is treated as the quantity to maximize, with repetition over a fixed set accepted as normal training practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Repetition is only informative when examples are real evidence; repeating synthetic scenes re-presents the renderer's quirks as if they were evidence, which is pure downside.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one fixed-dataset run against one streaming run at matched compute on one dense task; the direction is visible from two runs.

one_line_idea: Renderer identity leaves shortcut fingerprints that models exploit, and mixing multiple renderers is a near-free domain-randomization axis stronger than texture randomization.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets are typically produced with a single rendering engine whose shading, anti-aliasing, and tone-mapping choices imprint consistent low-level statistics on every image.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on single-renderer data learn renderer-specific shortcuts that fail on real images, and re-rendering the same scenes through multiple engines forces renderer-invariant features, yielding transfer gains larger than conventional texture randomization at similar cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched scene content, multi-renderer training will beat single-renderer training on real-data transfer, a renderer-identity classifier will show high separability of single-renderer data (confirming the shortcut surface), and the gain will exceed that of texture randomization applied within one renderer.
why_important: Re-rendering existing scene assets through additional engines is cheap compared to creating content, so a strong effect would be one of the best cost-benefit interventions available.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Randomization literature varies scene parameters within one engine; cross-engine ensembling as a first-class randomization axis may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render one scene corpus through several engines, train on single-engine versus mixed-engine subsets at matched size, and evaluate real-data transfer alongside renderer-classifier separability.
main_risk: Engines differ in supported content features, so scene-content parity across engines requires restricting to a common feature subset.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The renderer is treated as a neutral tool, with domain gap attributed to content and material choices rather than to engine identity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Anything constant across an entire training set becomes an invariant the model relies on, and engine statistics are the most constant thing in a single-engine dataset.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small classifier to distinguish two engines' renders of similar content; near-perfect separability confirms the shortcut surface exists before any transfer experiments.

one_line_idea: Tasks defined only through synthetic supervision, like intrinsic decomposition, may have models that learned renderer conventions rather than physics, and a real-light-transport audit would expose the gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some vision tasks (intrinsic image decomposition, material estimation, illumination estimation) rely almost entirely on synthetic ground truth because the quantities are unmeasurable in real scenes at scale, so models and metrics co-evolve inside the renderer's world.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models for such tasks fit the specific approximations of the generating renderer (its shading model, light-transport shortcuts) rather than physical structure, so they degrade systematically on real scenes with measured ground truth and on synthetic scenes from physically different renderers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating renderer-trained intrinsic-decomposition models on small physically measured real datasets and on cross-renderer synthetic tests will reveal errors aligned with the training renderer's known approximations, larger than within-renderer evaluation suggests.
why_important: These task communities may be optimizing convention-fitting for years without an external check; an audit either validates the enterprise or redirects it toward physically grounded evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cross-dataset checks exist, but a systematic renderer-convention audit with physically measured references may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on data from renderers with different light-transport fidelity, cross-evaluate, and anchor with a small physically measured real benchmark where obtainable.
main_risk: Physically measured references are tiny and domain-limited, so statistical power for the real-scene arm is inherently low.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic ground truth for physical quantities is treated as truth, with renderer approximation error assumed negligible relative to model error.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When the supervisor and the examiner are the same simulator, nothing in the loop can detect the simulator's own systematic errors.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Cross-evaluate two public intrinsic-decomposition models trained on different synthetic sources against each other's test sets; a large asymmetric drop signals convention-fitting immediately.

one_line_idea: Layout realism (object co-occurrence and physical support relations) transfers more than appearance realism, so scene-grammar investment beats shading investment at equal cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Procedural scene generation commonly places objects with simplified randomness while investing heavily in material and lighting fidelity, though real scenes have strong co-occurrence, support, and functional-arrangement structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models consume contextual priors from training scenes, so violating layout statistics injects wrong priors that hurt transfer more than flat shading does, making scene-grammar quality the higher-return realism axis.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Crossing layout realism (grammar-driven versus random placement) with appearance realism (high versus low shading fidelity) will show larger real-data transfer effects along the layout axis for detection and segmentation, with context-dependent classes driving the difference.
why_important: Scene grammars are software, shading is compute; if grammar wins, better synthetic data is cheaper than the field assumes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Context effects in perception are known; a cost-normalized factorial of layout-versus-appearance realism in synthetic data generation may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate the four factorial datasets with one asset library, train matched models, and evaluate on real data with per-class analysis separating context-dependent from context-independent classes.
main_risk: Grammar-driven placement reduces layout diversity if the grammar is too rigid, potentially conflating realism with reduced variety.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Realism means visual fidelity; placement plausibility is treated as an aesthetic nicety rather than a transfer-relevant factor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern backbones are trained to tolerate appearance variation but consume context statistics as priors, so the axis nobody randomizes is the axis that transfers.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare context-dependent class performance between grammar-placed and randomly-placed synthetic training at one fidelity level; two runs and a per-class breakdown.

one_line_idea: Procedural generation parameters can be optimized directly against downstream validation performance with black-box methods, because the loss over generation parameters is smoother than assumed.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Procedural pipelines expose dozens of distribution parameters (object counts, scale ranges, lighting distributions, clutter levels) that are set by intuition and rarely revisited, since evaluating one setting requires a full train-evaluate cycle.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream validation performance varies smoothly over generation parameters, so sample-efficient black-box optimization with cheap proxy trainings (small models, short schedules) can find substantially better parameter settings than expert defaults within a modest number of cycles.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Optimized generation parameters found via proxy-training black-box search will transfer to full-scale training with meaningful gains over expert defaults, and the measured response surface will show smooth low-effective-dimension structure justifying the approach.
why_important: This converts dataset design from craft into optimization, and the proxy-to-full transfer question it answers applies to every synthetic pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Simulator-parameter learning exists for narrow cases; a general demonstration with proxy-fidelity analysis and effective-dimension characterization may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one procedural pipeline with a parameter space, run black-box optimization using proxy trainings against a real validation set, and verify the winner transfers to full-scale training against the default configuration.
main_risk: Proxy trainings may misrank parameter settings whose value appears only at scale, breaking the outer optimization silently.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generation parameters are treated as domain-expert choices too expensive to optimize empirically.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distribution parameters act on the loss through millions of averaged samples, and averaging is exactly what makes response surfaces smooth and optimizable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Perturb two generation parameters over a small grid with proxy trainings and check whether the proxy response surface is smooth and reproducible across seeds before investing in the full loop.

one_line_idea: Camera and ISP simulation parameters matter more for geometric-task transfer than scene content, and calibrating the virtual camera to the target device closes more depth-estimation gap than content matching.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic pipelines model scene content in detail while using idealized pinhole cameras with default post-processing, though real deployment cameras impose distortion, rolling shutter, noise, and ISP transforms that geometric tasks are sensitive to.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For depth, pose, and structure tasks, the mismatch between idealized virtual cameras and real device pipelines is a first-order transfer factor, so calibrating simulation to the target camera (intrinsics, distortion, ISP) yields larger gains than equivalent effort on content realism.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A camera-calibrated synthetic variant will beat a content-upgraded variant of equal cost on real-device geometric evaluations, and the gain will track the degree of camera mismatch across several target devices.
why_important: Camera calibration is a per-device one-time cost measured in hours, versus content upgrades measured in artist-months; the leverage comparison directly reallocates pipeline effort.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] ISP simulation exists in isolation; a leverage comparison against content realism for geometric transfer may be unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one target device, produce camera-calibrated and content-upgraded synthetic variants at matched cost, train matched geometric models, and evaluate on data captured with that device.
main_risk: Gains may be device-specific and vanish when the deployment fleet spans heterogeneous cameras, requiring a distribution-over-devices formulation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The virtual camera is treated as a neutral observer, with transfer effort directed at what is in front of the lens rather than the lens itself.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Geometric tasks read their signal from exactly the image-formation properties (projection, distortion, noise floors) that idealized cameras get wrong everywhere in every frame.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Add measured lens distortion and sensor noise of one device to an existing synthetic depth dataset, retrain, and compare device-specific evaluation against the unmodified baseline in two runs.

one_line_idea: Rendered-human training data shows an uncanny-valley non-monotonicity: mid-realism renders transfer worse than either stylized or high-realism renders for person-centric tasks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic human datasets span a realism continuum from stylized game characters to scanned-avatar renders, and realism level is chosen by availability rather than by measured transfer value.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Transfer to real person-centric tasks is non-monotone in realism: stylized data teaches transferable structure without competing appearance cues, high-realism data matches real appearance, but mid-realism data creates features aligned with neither distribution, producing a measurable performance dip.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training pose and person-segmentation models across a controlled realism ladder will produce a U-shaped transfer curve with the trough at intermediate realism, robust across tasks and backbones.
why_important: Most affordable human-rendering pipelines sit exactly in the mid-realism range; if that range is a trap, procurement guidance for human-centric synthetic data changes materially.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Uncanny-valley effects are documented for human perception; an analogous non-monotonicity for model training value may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a realism ladder from one body model (stylized shading through scanned textures), train matched models per rung, and evaluate on real benchmarks, testing for the interior minimum.
main_risk: Realism ladders confound multiple factors (texture, geometry detail, animation quality), so the ladder needs single-factor rungs to attribute the dip.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Transfer value is assumed monotone in realism, making mid-realism a safe cost-quality compromise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature learning cares about distributional alignment, not human aesthetic comfort, and mid-realism data is distributionally farthest from both the stylized regime the model could ignore and the real regime it must serve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three rungs (stylized, intermediate, scanned) with one pose model each; the presence or absence of an interior dip is visible from three runs.

one_line_idea: Generator quality metrics like distribution-distance scores are nearly uncorrelated with the training utility of generated data, and the field needs utility-specific metrics rather than borrowed perceptual ones.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets are advertised with generator-quality metrics designed for perceptual evaluation (distribution distances in a fixed feature space), while their purpose is training downstream models, a different objective.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across generators, sampling configurations, and curation choices, perceptual distribution metrics rank synthetic datasets in an order weakly related to their measured training utility, because utility depends on coverage, label alignment, and redundancy that perceptual metrics compress or ignore.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A rank-correlation audit between perceptual metric scores and student-performance outcomes across many synthetic dataset variants will find low correlation, with systematic inversions where high-fidelity low-coverage sets score well perceptually but train poorly.
why_important: Procurement and research decisions are being made on metrics that may not measure the purchased quantity; establishing the disconnect forces the development of utility-honest reporting.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Complaints about perceptual metrics exist; a systematic utility-rank-correlation audit across diverse dataset variants may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Produce many synthetic dataset variants varying generator, guidance, curation, and diversity, compute perceptual metrics for each, train matched students on each, and report the metric-utility rank correlation.
main_risk: Utility is task-dependent, so the audit needs several downstream tasks to avoid replacing one over-general metric with another.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Better perceptual scores are assumed to indicate better synthetic training data, and dataset releases lead with those numbers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perceptual metrics reward matching the typical set, while training utility often lives in the atypical tail; the two objectives diverge by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take three dataset variants with clearly ordered perceptual scores and train one student on each; a single inversion in the utility ordering already undermines the metric's use as a proxy.

one_line_idea: Train-on-synthetic-test-on-real rankings of synthetic datasets flip across student architectures, so dataset-superiority claims made with one architecture are architecture-conditional statements in disguise.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] The standard protocol for comparing synthetic datasets trains one chosen student architecture on each dataset and compares real-test performance, implicitly assuming the ranking is architecture-independent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Synthetic datasets differ in which model inductive biases their artifacts and distribution choices interact with, so dataset rankings measured with different student families (convolutional, attention-based, different capacities) disagree materially.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Evaluating several synthetic datasets across a grid of student architectures will produce dataset-by-architecture interactions large enough to flip published-style rankings, with rank correlations across architectures well below 1.
why_important: Dataset papers and procurement decisions generalize from single-architecture evidence; quantifying ranking instability determines how much weight such claims can bear.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Architecture sensitivity is acknowledged informally; a systematic ranking-stability study for synthetic training data may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross several public synthetic datasets with several student families at matched training budgets, evaluate on common real benchmarks, and quantify ranking stability and interaction effect sizes.
main_risk: Fair budget matching across architectures is nontrivial, and unmatched tuning could masquerade as dataset-architecture interaction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A synthetic dataset that wins with one reasonable student is assumed to be the better dataset in general.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic artifacts are model-visible patterns, and different architectures are differently susceptible to exploiting or ignoring specific pattern families.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two datasets, two architectures, four runs; a single ranking flip at this scale justifies the full grid.

one_line_idea: A cheap probe suite over frozen foundation features can predict the full-training utility of a synthetic dataset, replacing most train-to-evaluate cycles in curation loops.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Measuring a synthetic dataset's value currently requires training models on it, which makes utility evaluation the bottleneck of every generation and curation iteration.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The information that determines full-training utility (coverage of the target distribution, label alignment, redundancy, artifact load) is measurable with lightweight probes over frozen pretrained features, yielding a predictor that ranks candidate datasets nearly as well as full training does.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A probe suite combining coverage, label-consistency, and redundancy measurements will achieve high rank agreement with full-training outcomes across diverse synthetic dataset variants, at orders-of-magnitude lower cost, with failure cases concentrated where probes and students use very different feature spaces.
why_important: Fast utility estimation would change generation pipelines from open-loop to closed-loop at iteration speeds currently impossible, compounding all other synthetic-data improvements.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual proxy signals exist; a validated composite probe suite positioned as a full-training surrogate for synthetic data may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble many synthetic dataset variants with known full-training outcomes, fit and validate the probe-suite predictor with proper held-out splits over generators and tasks, and characterize where it fails.
main_risk: The predictor may overfit the dataset-variant families it was validated on, silently breaking on novel generation paradigms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Training utility is assumed to be measurable only by training, making dataset evaluation inherently expensive.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Utility is a functional of distributional properties, and distributional properties are exactly what frozen-feature statistics estimate well without any training.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For ten dataset variants with existing training outcomes, compute three cheap probe statistics and check the achievable rank correlation in a day of feature extraction.

one_line_idea: Synthetic test sets systematically compress model rankings because generators regress toward typical instances, making synthetic evaluation optimistically biased and rank-unstable for model comparison.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data is increasingly proposed for evaluation (privacy-preserving benchmarks, coverage-controlled test suites), assuming generated tests can substitute for real ones in comparing models.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Generators produce instances closer to distribution modes than real sampling does at matched nominal difficulty, so synthetic test sets under-represent the tail cases that differentiate strong models, compressing measured gaps and destabilizing rankings relative to real tests.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Comparing model cohorts on paired real and synthetic test sets built for the same specification will show systematically smaller between-model gaps on synthetic tests and reduced ranking agreement with real-test outcomes, with the disagreement concentrated among top models.
why_important: If synthetic evaluation cannot separate top models, its adoption for benchmarking would freeze progress measurement exactly where precision matters most.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Synthetic evaluation proposals exist; a systematic ranking-fidelity audit against paired real tests may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired real and synthetic test sets under a common content specification, evaluate a diverse model cohort on both, and compare gap magnitudes, ranking agreement, and tail-case representation.
main_risk: Pairing real and synthetic tests fairly is hard, and specification mismatches could produce the predicted pattern for uninteresting reasons.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A synthetic test set matching a specification is assumed to measure the same thing as a real test set matching that specification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model separation lives in the tails, and mode-seeking generation is structurally worst at exactly the tails.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three models of known real-test ordering on one existing synthetic benchmark of the same task and check for gap compression immediately.

one_line_idea: Synthetic data quality is two independent axes, fidelity and coverage, that trade off differently per task, and single-scalar quality reporting systematically misleads adoption decisions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic datasets are compared with scalar quality summaries, though generation methods differ in whether they spend their error budget on per-sample realism (fidelity) or on distribution breadth (coverage).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream tasks weight fidelity and coverage differently (dense recognition favoring coverage, fine-grained discrimination favoring fidelity), so scalar rankings routinely recommend the wrong dataset for a given task, and two-axis reporting would flip a measurable fraction of adoption decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Decomposing dataset quality into fidelity and coverage estimates and mapping task performance over that plane will reveal task-dependent iso-performance contours with different slopes, such that scalar rankings disagree with task-optimal choices in many cells.
why_important: Adoption decisions are the practical output of dataset evaluation; a reporting change that prevents systematically wrong choices is directly actionable for the whole field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Fidelity-coverage decompositions exist for generator evaluation; connecting them to task-conditional training-data choice with decision-flip quantification may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate dataset variants spanning the fidelity-coverage plane via guidance and truncation controls, train matched models for several task types on each, and map per-task performance contours over the plane.
main_risk: Fidelity and coverage estimators share a feature space and are not perfectly independent, blurring the plane's axes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dataset quality is treated as a one-dimensional property that better generation methods increase uniformly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two axes are controlled by different generation knobs and consumed by different aspects of learning, so no single scalar can encode the decision-relevant information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Vary one guidance parameter to produce a high-fidelity-low-coverage and a low-fidelity-high-coverage variant, train two tasks on both, and check for the predicted preference reversal in four runs.

one_line_idea: Generators have seen the benchmarks: synthetic training data leaks evaluation content through generator memorization, inflating synthetic-data results in ways standard contamination checks never audit.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Text-to-image generators are trained on web-scale corpora that overlap with the sources of vision benchmarks, and synthetic-data experiments treat generated images as contamination-free because their pixels are new.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Prompting generators in the semantic vicinity of benchmark content produces training images that leak test-set-specific information (near-duplicate compositions, distinctive instances), measurably inflating benchmark scores of models trained on such synthetic data.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A leakage audit will find benchmark-adjacent generations at nonzero rates under natural prompting, and students trained with leak-heavy versus leak-scrubbed synthetic data will show score differences on the affected benchmarks but not on fresh evaluation data.
why_important: Synthetic data is being adopted partly to escape contamination concerns; demonstrating a laundering pathway through the generator would change evaluation hygiene requirements across the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Generator memorization is established; its quantified downstream effect on benchmark inflation via synthetic training data may be unaudited.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic training data with natural task prompts, run near-duplicate retrieval against benchmark test splits, scrub matches, train students on scrubbed versus unscrubbed data, and compare benchmark versus fresh-data performance.
main_risk: Semantic near-duplicate detection has threshold ambiguity, and the leak rate may vary enormously across benchmarks and prompting styles.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generated images are assumed contamination-free because they are not copies of any real file.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memorization means the generator can emit information about specific training items, and benchmarks live in that training set; novelty of pixels is irrelevant to information leakage.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Prompt one generator with class names of one benchmark and retrieve nearest test-set neighbors; visible near-duplicates in an afternoon establish the pathway.

one_line_idea: Reported synthetic-data gains are confounded by asymmetric tuning effort, and equal-tuning-budget re-evaluation would deflate a measurable share of published improvements.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers proposing synthetic-data pipelines tune generation parameters, mixing ratios, and training recipes for their method, while baselines are typically run at default or lightly tuned settings, a pattern documented in other subfields as a source of inflated gains.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under matched hyperparameter search budgets for both arms, a substantial fraction of published synthetic-data improvements shrinks or disappears, and the surviving gains identify the subset of techniques with real effect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-evaluating a sample of published synthetic-data results with symmetric tuning protocols will reduce the median reported gain noticeably, with shrinkage correlating with the original paper's baseline-tuning opacity.
why_important: Meta-corrections of this kind have repeatedly recalibrated subfields; synthetic data is due for one before its conclusions are cemented into industrial practice.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Equal-tuning audits exist in other areas; a systematic one for synthetic-data claims may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select representative published synthetic-data results with available code, define a symmetric tuning budget, re-run both arms, and report the gain-shrinkage distribution.
main_risk: Reproduction fidelity disputes are inevitable, and the audit needs preregistered protocols to be credible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Published synthetic-data gains are taken at face value as method effects rather than tuning-asymmetry effects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synthetic pipelines add many new tunable degrees of freedom, and every added degree of freedom is an opportunity for asymmetric optimization to masquerade as improvement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one prominent result, give the baseline the same tuning budget the pipeline received, and measure the surviving gain in a handful of runs.

one_line_idea: Per-image accounting hides the cost of synthetic data: under per-FLOP accounting that includes generation compute, many synthetic-data results are net-negative versus simply training longer on real data.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic-data comparisons equalize image counts or training steps while excluding the substantial compute spent generating the images, so the reported comparisons answer a question no budget-constrained practitioner actually faces.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When total compute (generation plus training) is the equalized resource, the synthetic-data advantage shrinks systematically, and for a meaningful class of settings the same compute spent on longer real-data training or stronger augmentation wins outright.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Re-running representative synthetic-augmentation setups under total-compute matching will flip a nontrivial fraction of positive results to neutral or negative, with the flips concentrated where generation cost per image is high relative to training cost.
why_important: Compute is the actual constraint in practice; accounting that ignores the generation bill systematically overstates synthetic data's practical value and misleads infrastructure decisions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cost caveats appear in discussions; a systematic total-compute-matched re-evaluation of synthetic-data claims may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several synthetic-augmentation settings, measure generation FLOPs, construct total-compute-matched real-only baselines (longer schedules, heavier augmentation, larger models), and compare outcomes at equal total budgets.
main_risk: Generation cost is amortizable across many downstream uses, so single-use accounting may be unfair to synthetic data in multi-project organizations.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Synthetic data comparisons at matched image counts are accepted as the standard fair protocol.
why_it_might_be_wrong: An intervention that costs compute must be benchmarked against other uses of that compute, and per-image protocols exempt synthetic data from exactly that comparison.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one published-style setup, give the real-only baseline extra training equal to the measured generation compute and see whether the synthetic advantage survives; two runs plus bookkeeping.

one_line_idea: Batch-generated synthetic data violates the i.i.d. assumption through shared seeds, prompts, and scheduler state, and decorrelating generation batches yields free training gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training theory and practice assume approximately independent samples, while synthetic data is produced in correlated batches (shared prompt templates, sequential seeds, common guidance settings) whose within-batch similarity is never audited.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Within-batch correlation in generated data reduces the effective sample size and injects correlated gradient noise, so generation protocols that enforce cross-batch decorrelation (seed spacing, prompt interleaving, setting jitter) improve downstream training at identical image counts.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measuring within-batch versus across-batch feature similarity will show substantial excess correlation under default generation, and students trained on decorrelated generations will outperform students trained on default generations at matched counts, with the gap growing at smaller dataset sizes.
why_important: This is a zero-cost protocol fix at generation time; if effective sample size is being silently wasted, every generative data pipeline is leaving performance on the table.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Correlation structure of generated corpora seems unexamined as a training-relevant property with a protocol-level remedy.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched corpora under default and decorrelated protocols from the same generator, quantify correlation structure in a fixed feature space, train matched students, and compare performance across dataset sizes.
main_risk: Decorrelation knobs may also change marginal image quality, requiring quality-matched controls to isolate the correlation effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generated images are implicitly treated as independent draws from the generator's distribution regardless of how the sampling loop was executed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Samplers are deterministic functions of highly structured inputs, and reusing structure across a batch mathematically cannot produce independent outputs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute within-batch versus across-batch embedding similarity for one default generation run; excess within-batch similarity is measurable in hours and gates the training experiment.

one_line_idea: Renderer labels are not ground truth for the evaluation convention: anti-aliased boundaries, transparency, and reflections are labeled by renderer logic that systematically disagrees with human annotation guidelines.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic labels are generated by renderer visibility logic (which surface owns a pixel), while human annotation guidelines resolve mixed pixels, transparent surfaces, and reflections by task-specific conventions; the two resolution rules are never reconciled.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Renderer label conventions disagree with annotation guidelines on a systematic pixel population (boundaries, glass, mirrors, thin structures), and this disagreement imposes a measurable ceiling on synthetic-trained model performance under human-convention evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] An audit comparing renderer labels against guideline-compliant human annotation of the same synthetic frames will find concentrated systematic disagreement on the predicted pixel populations, and convention-corrected synthetic labels will lift real-benchmark performance of synthetic-trained models on those populations.
why_important: The assumption that rendered labels are perfect is foundational to the entire synthetic-data enterprise; quantifying where it fails defines the true label-quality budget of simulation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual issues like transparency labeling are known irritations; a systematic renderer-versus-guideline disagreement audit with downstream impact measurement may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Have annotators label sampled synthetic frames under a real benchmark's guidelines, quantify disagreement with renderer labels by pixel population, then train with corrected labels and measure the recovered performance.
main_risk: Human annotation of synthetic frames imports human noise, so disagreement must be separated into systematic convention differences and ordinary annotator variance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Rendered labels are called ground truth without qualification, and label error is assumed to be an exclusively real-data problem.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visibility logic and human convention are different functions that provably diverge on optically complex pixels, and dense metrics integrate over exactly those pixels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inspect renderer labels on glass, mirrors, and thin structures for one synthetic dataset against the target benchmark's written guidelines; cataloguing systematic divergences takes one afternoon.

one_line_idea: More realism is not monotonically better: past a threshold, realistic synthesis re-imports the real world's spurious correlations that cruder randomized data had removed, hurting robustness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real datasets contain spurious correlations (context-object coupling, texture shortcuts) that harm robustness, and low-realism randomized synthetic data breaks many of them by construction, while the community pursues maximal realism as an unquestioned goal.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Part of synthetic data's value is inadvertent bias removal, so as synthesis approaches full realism it restores the real distribution's shortcuts, producing a non-monotone robustness curve where intermediate randomization outperforms maximal realism on out-of-distribution evaluation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping realism-versus-randomization while evaluating both in-distribution and shift-robustness metrics will show in-distribution performance rising with realism while robustness peaks at intermediate randomization, with the divergence traceable to reinstated context and texture shortcuts.
why_important: The realism-maximizing roadmap that guides simulation investment may be optimizing in-distribution scores at the direct expense of the robustness synthetic data was supposed to provide.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Randomization-for-invariance is known; the framing of realism as shortcut-restoration with a measured non-monotonicity may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a realism ladder where known spurious correlations of the target domain are measurably present or broken per rung, train matched models per rung, and evaluate in-distribution accuracy alongside shortcut-sensitivity probes and shift robustness.
main_risk: Quantifying shortcut presence in training data requires committing to specific shortcut hypotheses, which may miss the correlations that actually matter.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The asymptote of synthetic data quality is assumed to be indistinguishability from real data, full stop.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Matching the real distribution exactly means matching its biases exactly, so a synthesis pipeline that can control bias is strictly more valuable than one that reproduces it faithfully.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare context-shortcut sensitivity (objects on unusual backgrounds) between models trained on randomized-context versus realistic-context synthetic data in two runs.

one_line_idea: Synthetic data optimized to match today's distribution is optimized for the wrong target when deployment shifts the distribution, and shift-anticipating synthesis beats distribution-matching synthesis.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data pipelines take the current real distribution as the matching target, while deployed systems face distributions altered by time, adaptation of users, and the system's own feedback effects.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For deployments with predictable shift structure (seasonal cycles, hardware upgrades, behavior adaptation), synthesizing data for plausible future distributions rather than the present one yields better performance over the deployment window, and the advantage is largest where retraining cadence is slow.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In settings with documented temporal shift, models trained with shift-anticipating synthetic mixtures will outperform distribution-matched ones on later time slices while conceding little on the training-time slice, measured over held-out temporal sequences.
why_important: Matching the present is an unexamined default; if anticipation wins under realistic shift, the target-selection step becomes a first-class design decision in every synthetic pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temporal robustness is studied for models; using synthesis specifically to pre-train for forecast distributions may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use datasets with timestamped sequences exhibiting real drift, build present-matched and forecast-matched synthetic augmentations, train matched models, and evaluate across subsequent time slices.
main_risk: Forecasting distribution shift is itself hard, and a wrong forecast could underperform the present-matching default, making the method's value contingent on forecast quality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The real distribution at collection time is treated as the definitionally correct synthesis target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training data determines performance during deployment, not during collection, and the two distributions demonstrably differ in any system that operates over time.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one dataset with known seasonal structure, compare present-matched versus season-shifted synthetic augmentation for a model evaluated on the next season's data; two runs decide the direction.

one_line_idea: Synthetic data is assumed privacy-safe by construction, but generator memorization leaks training individuals, and the utility cost of verified non-memorization is unknown and possibly severe.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data is marketed as a privacy solution because generated records are not copies of real ones, while generative models demonstrably memorize and can reproduce near-copies of training samples under some conditions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For visual data containing people and identifiable scenes, the achievable frontier between measured re-identification risk and downstream utility is materially worse than assumed, and enforcing verified non-memorization (filtering or training constraints) costs a quantifiable, possibly large, share of the synthetic data's utility.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Mapping the risk-utility frontier by varying memorization-mitigation strength will show utility declining substantially before re-identification risk reaches levels that privacy claims imply, and unmitigated pipelines will exhibit nonzero measurable leakage.
why_important: Institutions are adopting synthetic data specifically for privacy compliance; an unmeasured risk-utility frontier means those decisions rest on an assumption rather than a measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Memorization and privacy are studied separately; a utility-annotated frontier for vision synthetic-data pipelines may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one generator trained on identifiable visual data, sweep mitigation strength, measure leakage with membership-inference and near-duplicate retrieval, train students per setting, and plot the joint risk-utility frontier.
main_risk: Leakage measurement methods have their own blind spots, and a clean-looking frontier could reflect weak auditing rather than actual safety.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Generated data is treated as anonymized by default because no real record appears verbatim.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Privacy is about information flow, not file identity, and memorization is precisely an information flow from training individuals to generated outputs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run near-duplicate retrieval from a generator's outputs back into its known training set at scale; nonzero verified matches establish the leak before any frontier mapping.

one_line_idea: The domain gap is treated as a scalar when it is a decomposable vector over appearance, content, sensor, and label-convention factors, and interventions are systematically misattributed as a result.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Papers report a single sim-to-real gap number and attribute its reduction to their intervention, though the gap aggregates several mechanistically distinct mismatch factors that different interventions address.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A factor-wise decomposition protocol (controlled swaps of appearance, content statistics, sensor pipeline, and label convention between synthetic and real) yields stable, additive-enough gap components, and re-analyzing standard interventions against components reveals widespread misattribution of their effects.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Component-wise measurement across dataset pairs will show interventions concentrating their effect on single components (translation on appearance, resampling on content), with published whole-gap narratives frequently crediting the wrong mechanism, and component profiles predicting intervention transfer across pairs.
why_important: A vector-valued gap converts sim-to-real research from anecdote comparison into mechanism accounting, letting practitioners diagnose before treating.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Individual factor studies exist; a standardized decomposition protocol with intervention re-attribution may not.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build controlled swap experiments for one synthetic-real pair (relight and retexture for appearance, resample for content, ISP transplant for sensor, convention transform for labels), measure component gaps, and re-evaluate representative interventions component-wise.
main_risk: Components interact (appearance changes affect content perception), so additivity is approximate and the protocol needs interaction terms to stay honest.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The gap is one number, and any method that shrinks it is understood to have addressed the domain gap as such.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distinct causal mechanisms cannot be diagnosed or treated through their sum, and every mature engineering field decomposes its error budgets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Implement two swaps (sensor ISP transplant and label-convention transform) on one pair and check whether their measured components are non-trivial fractions of the whole gap.

one_line_idea: Generation vintage is a hidden curriculum: synthetic corpora accumulate quality drift as pipelines improve, and ordering training by vintage versus shuffling changes outcomes, an unexamined degree of freedom.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Large synthetic corpora are accumulated over months of pipeline evolution (generator upgrades, prompt improvements, filter changes), producing systematic quality and distribution drift across the corpus that training treats as exchangeable data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Vintage drift is large enough that sample order and vintage-conditioned weighting materially affect final models: shuffling hides a drift signal that could be exploited (curriculum from old to new, or downweighting obsolete vintages) or that silently harms reproducibility when ignored.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Auditing an accumulated corpus will reveal measurable vintage-correlated distribution shifts, and training runs differing only in vintage ordering or weighting will differ beyond seed noise, with newest-vintage-weighted training winning on current evaluations.
why_important: Organizations sit on accumulated synthetic corpora and assume exchangeability; a vintage effect changes both how to train on them and how to interpret historical experiments run at different corpus states.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-vintage effects are discussed for web crawls; the internal vintage structure of accumulated synthetic corpora may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a corpus with generation-time metadata, quantify vintage drift in a fixed feature space, and run matched trainings under shuffled, chronological, reverse-chronological, and vintage-weighted regimes.
main_risk: Vintage correlates with content changes made deliberately (new prompt themes), so drift must be separated into pipeline drift and intentional content evolution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A synthetic corpus is treated as a bag of exchangeable samples regardless of when and how each sample was produced.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every pipeline change moves the generated distribution, and months of accumulated changes cannot leave the corpus exchangeable; the only question is whether training is sensitive to it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Embed samples from the oldest and newest vintage of one accumulated corpus and measure their separability with a simple classifier; strong separability confirms the premise in hours.

one_line_idea: The student-cannot-exceed-teacher assumption fails for dense geometry: averaging noisy generator-derived labels across many views or samples lets students surpass their labeling teacher measurably.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Auto-labeling pipelines assume the student's accuracy is bounded by the teacher's, and dense geometric labels (depth, correspondence) derived from teachers are noisy per-sample, while multiple correlated estimates per scene point are often available across views and samples.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When teacher errors are partly independent across views, augmentations, or samples of the same underlying geometry, aggregate supervision (multi-view consistency fusing many noisy teacher estimates) carries more information than any single teacher output, letting students exceed teacher accuracy in a predictable regime defined by error correlation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Students trained on consistency-fused teacher labels will exceed the teacher's own accuracy on held-out real geometry benchmarks, with the exceedance margin tracking the measured independence of teacher errors across views, and vanishing when errors are fully correlated.
why_important: This identifies the exact condition under which auto-labeling escapes the distillation ceiling, turning a folklore impossibility into an engineering criterion for label-fusion pipeline design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Multi-view fusion and distillation are both standard; framing and measuring teacher-exceedance as a function of error-correlation structure in dense labeling may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a teacher to produce per-view depth estimates over multi-view real scenes, fuse them with geometric consistency, train a student on fused labels, and compare student versus teacher accuracy on independent ground truth, alongside measured cross-view error correlation.
main_risk: Teacher errors are often systematically shared across views (textureless regions), which caps the achievable exceedance and may confine the effect to favorable scene types.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A student trained on a teacher's outputs is assumed to be at best a compressed copy, never more accurate than its supervision source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging partially independent noisy measurements provably reduces error, and geometry provides the consistency constraints that turn many bad labels into one good one.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On scenes with available ground truth, compare raw teacher depth against multi-view-fused teacher depth; if fusion already beats the raw teacher, the information headroom for the student is established without training.

one_line_idea: Real and synthetic data follow different scaling exponents that interact, and a two-term joint scaling law fitted from pilot runs predicts the optimal real-synthetic mix at any budget.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Scaling laws are fitted for single-source corpora, while practitioners face two-source budget decisions (how much real, how much synthetic) with no quantitative model of how the sources combine.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Real-data volume, synthetic-data volume, and their interaction determine loss through a stable parametric surface (task-dependent exponents plus a substitution term), fittable from small pilot grids and extrapolable to larger budgets with useful accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Joint scaling fits from pilot-scale grids will predict held-out large-budget mixed-training outcomes within tolerances that make mix-selection reliable, and the fitted substitution elasticity between real and synthetic data will vary systematically by task type.
why_important: A validated mixing law converts synthetic-data budgeting from sweep-based guesswork into a forecastable engineering computation, at exactly the scales where sweeps are unaffordable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Data-mixing scaling work exists for language corpora; a validated real-synthetic joint law for vision tasks with substitution-elasticity interpretation may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a pilot grid over real and synthetic volumes for several tasks, fit candidate two-source laws, and validate extrapolation against held-out larger-budget runs including the predicted optimal mixes.
main_risk: Synthetic data quality is heterogeneous, and a law fitted for one generator configuration may not transfer to another without refitting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixing decisions are assumed to require empirical sweeps at the target scale because the sources interact unpredictably.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scaling regularity has held across every data regime where it has been carefully measured, and two-source training is a modest extension of measured territory.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fit the law on a small grid for one task and test its prediction at one point outside the grid; a week of small runs establishes whether the functional form holds.

one_line_idea: Synthetic-data returns plateau when the student saturates the generator's effective support, and the intrinsic dimension of the generated set predicts the plateau point before training reaches it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Adding synthetic data shows diminishing returns at some scale, but the plateau point is discovered empirically per project, with no predictive quantity that anticipates where more generation stops paying.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The plateau occurs when training has consumed the generator's effective support (the data manifold it can actually produce), so support-size measures (intrinsic dimension estimates, coverage growth curves of generated sets) predict the saturation scale independently of the student's architecture.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across generators of different diversity, the synthetic-data scale at which student improvement plateaus will correlate strongly with measured effective-support statistics of the generated corpus, and truncation interventions that shrink support will shift the plateau earlier by the predicted amount.
why_important: A pre-training plateau predictor tells teams when to stop paying for generation and switch budget to real collection or generator improvement, a recurring high-stakes decision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Diminishing returns are universally observed; a validated support-based predictor of the saturation scale may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several generator configurations with measurable support statistics, train students across a data-scale ladder, locate plateaus, and test the support-statistic correlation plus the truncation-shift prediction.
main_risk: Intrinsic-dimension estimators are notoriously sensitive to feature space and scale choices, and a fragile estimator would produce an unfalsifiable moving target.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Diminishing returns are attributed loosely to data quality limits, with the plateau treated as an empirical surprise each time.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A student cannot keep learning from a source that has no more distinct content to show, so saturation must be governed by some measure of the source's content capacity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare plateau points of one student trained on a truncation-limited versus a full-diversity variant of the same generator; the ordering is checkable with two data ladders.

one_line_idea: The true unit cost of synthetic data is dominated by curation, validation, and integration rather than generation, and total-cost accounting reverses several published cost-benefit claims.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Synthetic data is promoted as cheap because per-image generation cost is low and falling, while the surrounding pipeline (filtering, label verification, convention alignment, dataset QA, mixing experiments) consumes engineering effort that no paper accounts for.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under honest total-cost-of-ownership accounting across real projects, the generation step is a minority of synthetic-data cost, and for a class of tasks the all-in cost per unit of performance gained exceeds that of straightforward real-data collection and annotation, reversing the headline economics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Instrumented case studies tracking all pipeline costs will show curation-validation dominating generation cost by a substantial factor, and the resulting cost-per-performance comparisons will flip the synthetic-versus-real verdict in a measurable fraction of studied settings.
why_important: Organizational adoption decisions cite per-image cost; if the decision-relevant number is several times larger, many adoption decisions are being made on the wrong arithmetic.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Cost discussions exist qualitatively; instrumented total-cost case studies with performance-normalized comparison may be absent from the literature.
